ABINGDON HERALD : SATURDAY 7 SEPTEMBER 1895

          ABINGDON CRICKET AND FOOTBALL
                    CLUB.
             CRICKET SEASON, 1895.

  Matches arranged: 21; played, 17; won, 8; lost, 7;
drawn, 2; scratched, 4. The averages of the 1st XI.
in both batting and bowling are appended:
  It will be noticed that the late captain, Mr. F. D.
Curtis, heads the batting list with an average of
24.50, Payne and Wilson coming next with 16.33
and 16.25 respectively, while Dandridge, Allen, W.
Legge, F. H. Pryce and Skurray all get into double
figures. Messrs. A. C. M. Croome and F. Deane
appeared once each, and scored over the century, 117
being Mr. Croome's score and 109 Mr. Deane's. In
the bowling Payne, Dandridge and H. S. Challenor
have borne the brunt, the former taking 27 wickets at
an average cost of 5.37 runs, Dandridge 49 at an
average of 7.97 runs, and Challenor 37 wickets at an
average of 9.02; all very good performances. Messrs.
W. T. Morland, Wilson, Lovett, Legge and Ward have
all rendered useful service in this department.
Though the 1st XI. have achieved successes over
Oxford City and Reading, they have not done so well
generally, as in other years. The worst feature of
this year's proceedings is the number of matches
scratched. This we consider a bad omen for the club,
as the reason given for the scratchings is the inability
of the officials to raise teams. This ought not to be
with any club having so many playing members on the
books. Each member is supplied with a fixture-list at
the beginning of the season, and as the success of the
club should be the first thought of all members we
greatly wonder at so many members engaging to play
other matches on dates fixed for the club matches, but
to this can be traced the falling off in the 1st XI. per-
formances. If all the subscribing members would pull
together, the Abingdon Cricket and Football Club
would never lack a team, either 1st or 2nd, that would
fail to uphold the honour of the club and the town
which supports it, and we hope in future there will
be no difficulty in this particular direction. We
heartily congratulate the club on the success it has
so far achieved and the members may be assured that
if the remedies prescribed are properly applied there
is a brilliant future in store.

             CRICKET SEASON, 1895.

  Matches arranged: 21; played, 17; won, 8; lost, 7;
drawn, 2; scratched, 4. The averages of the 1st XI.
in both batting and bowling are appended:
  It will be noticed that the late captain, Mr. F. D.
Curtis, heads the batting list with an average of
24.50, Payne and Wilson coming next with 16.33
and 16.25 respectively, while Dandridge, Allen, W.
Legge, F. H. Pryce and Skurray all get into double
figures. Messrs. A. C. M. Croome and F. Deane
appeared once each, and scored over the century, 117
being Mr. Croome's score and 109 Mr. Deane's. In
the bowling Payne, Dandridge and H. S. Challenor
have borne the brunt, the former taking 27 wickets at
an average cost of 5.37 runs, Dandridge 49 at an
average of 7.97 runs, and Challenor 37 wickets at an
average of 9.02; all very good performances. Messrs.
W. T. Morland, Wilson, Lovett, Legge and Ward have
all rendered useful service in this department.
Though the 1st XI. have achieved successes over
Oxford City and Reading, they have not done so well
generally, as in other years. The worst feature of
this year's proceedings is the number of matches
scratched. This we consider a bad omen for the club,
as the reason given for the scratchings is the inability
of the officials to raise teams. This ought not to be
with any club having so many playing members on the
books. Each member is supplied with a fixture-list at
the beginning of the season, and as the success of the
club should be the first thought of all members we
greatly wonder at so many members engaging to play
other matches on dates fixed for the club matches, but
to this can be traced the falling off in the 1st XI. per-
formances. If all the subscribing members would pull
together, the Abingdon Cricket and Football Club
would never lack a team, either 1st or 2nd, that would
fail to uphold the honour of the club and the town
which supports it, and we hope in future there will
be no difficulty in this particular direction. We
heartily congratulate the club on the success it has
so far achieved and the members may be assured that
if the remedies prescribed are properly applied there
is a brilliant future in store.

               THE SECOND ELEVEN
although not so successful this year as last, have been
able to win more matches than they have lost, and in
three cases out of five, had time permitted the drawn
games to be played out the gains would most probably
have been increased. The batting averages show a
slight falling off. Jackson, who last year had an
average of 22, takes second place with 15, but
Glanville and Steptoe show marked improvement.
Heath carries off the honours, but he has only played
in six innings. There are several young players who
claim attention, and it would be well for older mem-
bers next season to look to these rising batsmen if
they wish the club to prosper. Matcham, who only
played three innings, was not out on each occasion,
and winds up with an average of 58: In the bowling
department a word of commendation is due to Glan-
ville, who has bowled admirably. Heath and Pryce
have both bowled well. If a great deal of the net
practice was abolished and scratch teams were got
together to practice, the fielding would be better. An
improvement in that respect is much needed, for if
the fielding had been smarter several matches could
have been pulled out of the fire this season. Matches
played, 12; won, 4; lost, 3; drawn, 5.

disputes.chosen: A. Smith and H. Hodgson started for Carlisle after the luncheon interval; but Pye quickly disposed of the first named, clean bowling him for a "duck." With Jackson in, runs came freely, both men batting confidently. At 36 Goodband relieved Butler, and carried Hodgson's bails away with his first delivery. Downey and Todd quickly followed in, and out, but J. G. Hodgson and Jackson made another good stand. At length, in trying to pull one from Goodband, Jackson got his leg in front of the wicket, and was out. His 40 was a capital display of cricket, for he played well all round, being equally as strong on the leg side as on the off; and he drove well along the ground. When Jackson fell the total stood at 99, and with the "century" up Irwin followed him out. Immediately afterwards J. G. Wilson missed Hodgson; and for a time it looked as if this mistake would cost the Tynesiders the match, but at 110 Pye beat Stordy, and two runs later got rid of McIlvena. Then Goodband joined in, and getting Quirk and Brooks for "blobs," finished off the innings for 115, leaving the home team victorious by eight runs. There were about 1,000 people on the ground during the afternoon. Score:—

The morning opened dull, and a slight shower of rain, following the storm of Saturday, made the pitch rather slow, and gave the bowlers great assistance. That the trundlers could get work on was quickly evident when once the game began, and all through the day the batsmen were compelled to watch the ball very carefully.
Captain Nicholl's team batted first, Tom Murphy and J G Wilson opening to the bowling of A Smith and McIlvena. The start was a disastrous one, Murphy being taken in the slips off a bumping ball which broke back, at 3; Wilson beaten by McIlvena at 10, and Butler also bowled at 16. Then H Haslam and Goodband, playing sound cricket, gradually carried the total to 93, before Goodband fell to a catch by McIlvena. The South Northumberland professional had played a free open game for 39. None of the succeeding batsmen could stay long with Haslam, who continued to score freely, and the whole side was out for 123. Haslam carried out his bat for a meritorious 51, in which he scarcely made a bad stroke, while his cutting was well-timed and hard.

ABINGDON HERALD: SATURDAY 24 AUGUST 1895-5
SPORTING NOTES.
(From our Oxford Correspondent.)
THURSDAY.
Cup-ties were numerous last week, and conse-
quently the cricket generally was fuller of interest
than usual. There were two important contests in the
semi-finals for the County Cup, but neither of them
produced any surprise except that perhaps the favourite
club won in each case rather easier than was expected.
The City and the Victoria attracted a goodly number
of spectators. The former won the toss, but it was
undoubtedly one of those few occasions when the right
thing was to put the opponents in, which was done.
The wicket was still difficult owing to the recent wet
weather, but the drying process was proceeding so
fast that there was every prospect of its improving
before the day was out.
In addition to other advantages, the City had in Case
a bowler who was quite new to the Victoria batsmen,
and so well did he take advantage of his opportunities
that a few minutes over the hour sufficed to dispose
of the whole of the Victoria team for 49 only. Case
had the remarkable analysis of nine wickets for 22
runs, and the great collapse of the Victoria batting
was the more unexpected as the club had been doing
pretty well of late. At this point it looked as if all
interest was gone out of the game, but the City started
in a more disastrous way than their opponents. Nutt
and Freeborn proved quite irresistible, and Day, Case,
Sheard and Phillips had all gone by the time 10
appeared on the telegraph. Moulder and A. W. Roberts
were then associated, but the score had not been
augmented by 20 before the former gave a chance in
the deep. This, however, was not accepted, and
proved the turning point of the game. The Victoria's
score was soon passed, and Moulder, playing faultless
cricket and putting plenty of power into his strokes,
finally amassed the fine total of 94. A. W. Roberts
also deserves great praise for his steady defensive play
at a critical time. Subsequently G. A. Roberts played
a good not-out innings of 23. An opinion was ex-
pressed that the Victoria did not bowl Freeborn enough,
an opinion which the figures in the analysis certainly
seem to confirm.
Cowley put almost the strongest team they could
raise into the field against Thame, who were also well
represented, D. C. Lee being about the only absentee.
By-the-way, the City and Victoria also had good
teams, though the former were the worst off with
Brownrigg and Gmelin absent against Hedges on the
other side. To return to the Cowley and Thame
match. Like the other, it attracted a fairly good
gathering of spectators, and as Cowley had first
innings the interest was kept up longer, though it
was felt from the start that the visitors were over-
matched.
Regarding the actual play, the brothers Rogers were
mainly responsible for the victory, though the batting
was by no means uneven throughout the team. Arnold
and P. Rogers made an excellent start, putting on 55
for the first wicket, but it might have been only half
that amount had a chance from P. Rogers at 27 been
accepted. Later on A. Rogers hit about vigorously and
put 40 to his credit, so that with useful scores from F.
and W. King, Burrin and Walker the total rose to 181.
At no time did Thame look like making a fight of it,
and the only stands made were for the second and fifth
wickets, Wells and Rowell putting on 21 for the former
and Rowell and Holloway 13 for the latter. Both the
Rogers were in dangerous moods, while W. King, who
took the ball later on, rattled out three men for only
five runs. For Thame, Messenger proved the most
successful bowler, and he might have had still more
work with advantage. In the batting, Rowell and
Holloway gave excellent displays considering the
trying circumstances.
The final for the County Cup will therefore have to
be fought out between Cowley and the City, which
were certainly the two strongest teams on paper that
entered the competition. A meeting of the committee
of the Association will be held to-morrow at the
"Golden Cross," at noon, when the place and date of
the final will be selected. It is generally expected
that the date will be September 2nd and 3rd, but the
selection of the ground is at present doubtful ; for my
own part I should say that one in Oxford would prove
far and away the most convenient and pay the best.
Still, of course, the consideration of keeping up the
interest in district centres cannot be ignored.
The County met with another reverse on Monday and Tuesday last, when they opposed the M.C.C. at Lord's. It can hardly be said that they in any way discredited themselves, for the premier club had got together a high-class eleven, with such first-class cricketers as Hornsby, Carpenter, Hewett, Dauglish, Mead, etc. To get such a side out for 158 was a capital performance, and reflects credit on the steady bowling of the brothers Rogers. Carlin was the only one to make any serious stand, and his 68 was got by excellent cricket. The visitors with Bradford (13) and Wells (22) made a fair start, but thereafter Woodcock and Mead carried all before them and the innings closed for 61, Woodcock's analysis of 8 overs, 1 maiden, 16 runs, and 5 wickets being the most remarkable performance of the match.
Following on our team did much better. Smith was
in his happiest vein, and playing a safe game obtained
the fine score of 42 not out. Wood also had his
revenge for being disposed of so cheaply in the first
innings, and scored 33 by means of some stylish
cricket. Bradford, Wells and Deane also put on useful
items, so that they managed to save the innings defeat
and set the M.C.C. 41 to get to win. These, however,
were obtained for the loss of only one wicket, and the
county had to put up with a nine wicket defeat.
There were two or three more City Cup matches on
during the past week, but I must own that I am rather
in a fog as to exactly how far the competition has
gone. The holders had a narrow shave of being
knocked out by the Clarendon Press last Saturday.
The Press batted first, and mainly by the assistance of
Simms and Eddles compiled 89. Nash was quite in
his best form and took nine wickets for 30. At the
commencement of the Corporation innings Wheeler
carried all before him, and five wickets fell in rapid
succession. Then Jennings made things lively, and
further assistance coming from R. Kimber and Tanner
the score reached 85 for nine wickets. At this point
the excitement naturally ran high. Tanner and
Thomas, however, managed to get the required runs,
and won the match for the holders by six.
In the match between Cowley 2nd XI. and the
College Servants 2nd XI., Colonel Ward, Captain
Lethbridge, and Goodey were all in good form for
Cowley, who finally amassed 122. Goodey proved even
more effective with the ball than the bat, and with
the exception of Knibbs and Allen the Servants made
a sorry show, and were all out for 57.
The St. Paul's and E.O.C.C. tie on Saturday proved
a striking reversal of a friendly contest which took
place on the Thursday previous. On that day the Con-
servatives made 104 and bowled their opponents out
for 26 only. Whereas on Saturday St. Paul's scored
176 for seven wickets and disposed of the E.O.C.C. for
63. For the parish club the scoring was consistently
good, but Mason (53) and Hart (40) gave the best
displays. Hedges proved the great stumbling block
to the Conservatives. Only Huggins (27), Bristowe
(11) and Weedon (10) could make anything of him,
and even these had to succumb to his onslaught in
the end. His analysis was the remarkable one of seven
wickets for 13 runs.
The D.A.C. have been rather under a cloud of late,
receiving defeats at the hands of St. Barnabas and Mr.
Holloway's XI. On Saturday, however, they did
better, and managed to gain a victory over Headington
Quarry by 23 runs. The match was full of incident.
In the first place the D.A.C. lost seven wickets for 29,
and then by some spirited play on the part of Dr.
Brooks (57) and patient defence, G. J. Haines and
Spurling totalled 108. Headington Quarry in reply
started pretty well, and had got 70 on the board for
the loss of only four wickets when a rot set in and
the whole side were out for 80.
The biennial meeting of the Oxford and Cambridge
Servants on the river and the cricket field took place
at the end of last week. Cambridge was the scene of
operations, and according to all accounts the Oxford
visitors were treated right royally during their three
days' stay. Besides the chief objects of the re-union
entertainments and amusements were provided con-
tinually. Unfortunately for Oxford they were unsuc-
cessful in the two great events, after an excellent
fight in both, the boat race being lost by three quarters
of a length and the cricket match by 10 runs. In the
latter contest it was undoubtedly the fine batting of
J. Stearn, Collins and Holt in the first innings which
gave Cambridge the victory. In the rowing the sinuous
course of the Cam appeared to bother the visiting cox
considerably, and is supposed to have lost his boat a
good deal.
On Saturday the Oxford Times C.C. broke the spell of
bad luck which has attended their annual matches
with Wheatley for some years past. The scoring was
low, so that the majority of 25 by which the O.T. won
was a fairly large margin. The winners owed their
success as much as anything to the great improvement
in their fielding, two or three very smart catches
being brought off.

ABINGDON HERALD: SATURDAY 24 AUGUST 1895-5
SPORTING NOTES.
(From our Oxford Correspondent.)
THURSDAY.
Cup-ties were numerous last week, and conse-
quently the cricket generally was fuller of interest
than usual. There were two important contests in the
semi-finals for the County Cup, but neither of them
produced any surprise except that perhaps the favourite
club won in each case rather easier than was expected.
The City and the Victoria attracted a goodly number
of spectators. The former won the toss, but it was
undoubtedly one of those few occasions when the right
thing was to put the opponents in, which was done.
The wicket was still difficult owing to the recent wet
weather, but the drying process was proceeding so
fast that there was every prospect of its improving
before the day was out.
In addition to other advantages, the City had in Case
a bowler who was quite new to the Victoria batsmen,
and so well did he take advantage of his opportunities
that a few minutes over the hour sufficed to dispose
of the whole of the Victoria team for 49 only. Case
had the remarkable analysis of nine wickets for 22
runs, and the great collapse of the Victoria batting
was the more unexpected as the club had been doing
pretty well of late. At this point it looked as if all
interest was gone out of the game, but the City started
in a more disastrous way than their opponents. Nutt
and Freeborn proved quite irresistible, and Day, Case,
Sheard and Phillips had all gone by the time 10
appeared on the telegraph. Moulder and A. W. Roberts
were then associated, but the score had not been
augmented by 20 before the former gave a chance in
the deep. This, however, was not accepted, and
proved the turning point of the game. The Victoria's
score was soon passed, and Moulder, playing faultless
cricket and putting plenty of power into his strokes,
finally amassed the fine total of 94. A. W. Roberts
also deserves great praise for his steady defensive play
at a critical time. Subsequently G. A. Roberts played
a good not-out innings of 23. An opinion was ex-
pressed that the Victoria did not bowl Freeborn enough,
an opinion which the figures in the analysis certainly
seem to confirm.
Cowley put almost the strongest team they could
raise into the field against Thame, who were also well
represented, D. C. Lee being about the only absentee.
By-the-way, the City and Victoria also had good
teams, though the former were the worst off with
Brownrigg and Gmelin absent against Hedges on the
other side. To return to the Cowley and Thame
match. Like the other, it attracted a fairly good
gathering of spectators, and as Cowley had first
innings the interest was kept up longer, though it
was felt from the start that the visitors were over-
matched.
Regarding the actual play, the brothers Rogers were
mainly responsible for the victory, though the batting
was by no means uneven throughout the team. Arnold
and P. Rogers made an excellent start, putting on 55
for the first wicket, but it might have been only half
that amount had a chance from P. Rogers at 27 been
accepted. Later on A. Rogers hit about vigorously and
put 40 to his credit, so that with useful scores from F.
and W. King, Burrin and Walker the total rose to 181.
At no time did Thame look like making a fight of it,
and the only stands made were for the second and fifth
wickets, Wells and Rowell putting on 21 for the former
and Rowell and Holloway 13 for the latter. Both the
Rogers were in dangerous moods, while W. King, who
took the ball later on, rattled out three men for only
five runs. For Thame, Messenger proved the most
successful bowler, and he might have had still more
work with advantage. In the batting, Rowell and
Holloway gave excellent displays considering the
trying circumstances.
The final for the County Cup will therefore have to
be fought out between Cowley and the City, which
were certainly the two strongest teams on paper that
entered the competition. A meeting of the committee
of the Association will be held to-morrow at the
"Golden Cross," at noon, when the place and date of
the final will be selected. It is generally expected
that the date will be September 2nd and 3rd, but the
selection of the ground is at present doubtful ; for my
own part I should say that one in Oxford would prove
far and away the most convenient and pay the best.
Still, of course, the consideration of keeping up the
interest in district centres cannot be ignored.
The County met with another reverse on Monday and Tuesday last, when they opposed the M.C.C. at Lord's. It can hardly be said that they in any way discredited themselves, for the premier club had got together a high-class eleven, with such first-class cricketers as Hornsby, Carpenter, Hewett, Dauglish, Mead, etc. To get such a side out for 158 was a capital performance, and reflects credit on the steady bowling of the brothers Rogers. Carlin was the only one to make any serious stand, and his 68 was got by excellent cricket. The visitors with Bradford (13) and Wells (22) made a fair start, but thereafter Woodcock and Mead carried all before them and the innings closed for 61, Woodcock's analysis of 8 overs, 1 maiden, 16 runs, and 5 wickets being the most remarkable performance of the match.
Following on our team did much better. Smith was
in his happiest vein, and playing a safe game obtained
the fine score of 42 not out. Wood also had his
revenge for being disposed of so cheaply in the first
innings, and scored 33 by means of some stylish
cricket. Bradford, Wells and Deane also put on useful
items, so that they managed to save the innings defeat
and set the M.C.C. 41 to get to win. These, however,
were obtained for the loss of only one wicket, and the
county had to put up with a nine wicket defeat.
There were two or three more City Cup matches on
during the past week, but I must own that I am rather
in a fog as to exactly how far the competition has
gone. The holders had a narrow shave of being
knocked out by the Clarendon Press last Saturday.
The Press batted first, and mainly by the assistance of
Simms and Eddles compiled 89. Nash was quite in
his best form and took nine wickets for 30. At the
commencement of the Corporation innings Wheeler
carried all before him, and five wickets fell in rapid
succession. Then Jennings made things lively, and
further assistance coming from R. Kimber and Tanner
the score reached 85 for nine wickets. At this point
the excitement naturally ran high. Tanner and
Thomas, however, managed to get the required runs,
and won the match for the holders by six.
In the match between Cowley 2nd XI. and the
College Servants 2nd XI., Colonel Ward, Captain
Lethbridge, and Goodey were all in good form for
Cowley, who finally amassed 122. Goodey proved even
more effective with the ball than the bat, and with
the exception of Knibbs and Allen the Servants made
a sorry show, and were all out for 57.

a striking reversal of a friendly contest which took
place on the Thursday previous. On that day the Con-
servatives made 104 and bowled their opponents out
for 26 only. Whereas on Saturday St. Paul's scored
176 for seven wickets and disposed of the E.O.C.C. for
63. For the parish club the scoring was consistently
good, but Mason (53) and Hart (40) gave the best
displays. Hedges proved the great stumbling block
to the Conservatives. Only Huggins (27), Bristowe
(11) and Weedon (10) could make anything of him,
and even these had to succumb to his onslaught in
the end. His analysis was the remarkable one of seven
wickets for 13 runs.

receiving defeats at the hands of St. Barnabas and Mr.
Holloway's XI. On Saturday, however, they did
better, and managed to gain a victory over Headington
Quarry by 23 runs. The match was full of incident.

operations, and according to all accounts the Oxford

tinually. Unfortunately for Oxford they were unsuc-

in their fielding, two or three very smart catches
being brought off.

CRICKET NOTES.
(By "Curtos.")

disputes.chosen:
(By "CASTOR.")
We are frequently told that what spectators like to see are
batsmen who make things lively for the bowlers; and, if this is
really so, those who saw the game between Captain Nicholls' and
Mr Bewicke's teams would enjoy themselves. Though both
Vin. Thompson and Butler played exceptionally well, their per-
formances were quite overshadowed by the doings of George Simp-
son, who, after taking seven wickets for 41 runs, scored 177, and
was not out at the close. So far as I could see, Simpson never
made a bad stroke until he had reached his hundred, and the
chance he gave to Butler at 110 was a difficult one for the fielder
to judge. The hitting was, as is usual with Simpson, beautifully
timed and clean, and none of the bowlers seemed to give him any
trouble, though Walters almost bowled him second ball. V.
Thompson's 89 was a capital display of steady cricket; and
Butler's 82 was obtained in his best style. There was a large
gathering of spectators in the field, and after such an interesting
game we may expect good crowds at the Constabulary Ground
throughout the remainder of the season.

In fact, what victories they have gained here have been chiefly over school boys, and were the best team chosen to play for Northumberland probably only our Borderer—R Spencer—would be sure of a place in it. At the present time several prominent county gentlemen are trying to improve cricket in these parts. Towards this end they are inviting strong southern teams to visit them; and sarcastic remarks about those connected with the game, and the players, from the pen of the Borderers' superior young man will not help them much. Perhaps, after all, it is not county so much as afternoon tea party—wickets that this critic patronises, while his own failing of in bowling he attributes to the weakness of local batsmen, as he can only bowl well against good men. What a pity he cannot play in the south.

C. Mortimer will, I believe, call a general meeting shortly, and lay the matter before it.

I notice that the Elswick Works Club has fixed their match with
Benwell on July 27 as Lisey's benefit game. A more capable and
painstaking professional cannot be found than Lisey, and as a
player he ranks among the best in the north. His bowling has
pulled the club through many of their engagements, and I am
sure every member will do his best to increase the fund to be
handed over to their professional, who, by his ability on the field
and conduct off, does as much as any one connected with it to
uphold its honour and dignity.
I hope my readers will not forget that the game between
South Northumberland and Elswick Works, at Gosforth, on
Saturday, is for the benefit of the professional Goodband. This
player is certainly one of the best we have ever had in the North
of England, and deserves a bumper gate.
On Saturday Stockton visited Darlington, and, thanks to
McDonald's 75 not out, defeated the home team easily. Lieut.
Coates had another day out against Durham School, and had
hard lines in missing his century by 7 runs; while his batting
was followed up by some good bowling on the part of Fergu-
son. The matches between South Shields and Tynemouth for
Copeland's benefit, furnished some good cricket, but ended in a
draw. Wallsend could do little with the bowling of Simpson (5
for 13) and Goodband (4 for 12), and were all out for 31. What
was the matter with North Durham on Saturday ? Did they all
get the "hump" together, for there was certainly something
wrong with them. For six of them to go down without scoring re-
quires some explanation.
Sunderland, though they succeeded in beating Consett at Con-
sett, could do no better than draw on Saturday at Sunderland;
though as the full five hours were not played I believe they
intend to claim the match. One of the best performances of the
day was that of Eley in the match against the Royal Grammar
School; for after taking seven wickets for 14 runs he came out
top scorer of his side with a well-played 28. Up to the beginning
of this month he had got 57 wickets for less than 6 runs each—a
bowling feat that will take some beating.
St. George's and Northumberland met on Saturday, in fine
weather, before a small gate. Northumberland batted first, and
were got rid of very cheaply for 113. Moss took five wickets;
Bell, three; and V. Thompson, two for 1 run. Hoare batted well
for 32. On St. George's going in a complete rot took place, and
they were all out in less than an hour for 38. Not the best form
was shown. Everyone seemed to think that because Thompson
got a duck there was no necessity for their getting any either.
This won't do. Their cracks cannot come off every time, and the
rest of the team must make up their minds to do a fair share in
the run getting. The fielding on both sides was very good.

Moss took five wickets; Bell, three; and V. Thompson, two for 1 run. Hoare batted well for 38 On St. George's going in a complete rot took place, and they were all out in less than an hour for 28. Not the best form ever seemed to think that because Thompson got a duck there was no necessity for their getting any other. This won't do. Their cracks cannot come off every time, and the rest of the team must make up their minds to do a fair share in the run getting. The fielding on both sides was very good.

MR BEWICKE'S XL v. NORTHERN NOMADS.
A two days' match between these teams commenced on the Close House Ground on Tuesday, and finished yesterday in a decisive victory for Mr Bewicke's eleven by an innings and 65 runs. Batting first on Tuesday, the home team made 264, the Rev E W R Walters playing a fine innings of 67; while Guttridge and Captain Wilkinson had for 55 and 45 respectively. After the Nomads had commenced well with Clayton and Mortimer, Guttridge and Walters quickly disposed of several of the other batsmen, and it was not until P Ashworth and Morton came together that a second effective stand was made. Both played steadily, but none of the others could do anything with the bowling, and the side were all out for 149. Following up, they fared badly against Guttridge and A A Mewburn, the professional getting four wickets for 32 runs, while Mewburn's four only cost 16 runs. The innings realised 49, P Ashworth and Clayton alone reaching double figures. SCORE:—

The preliminary rounds of this competition having been duly played off it only remains for Presteign to meet Worcester St. John's in the final at Widemarsh to-day (Saturday), to decide the destination of the Cup. Two seasons ago, it may be remembered, St. John's were returned the winners, but last year the holders were defeated by Lugwardine. However, in the first round this season St. John's reversed this decision, somewhat easily defeating the strong team the Lugwardine Cricket Club had brought against them. With both teams who play in to-day's final so strongly represented, an excellently contested game should take place. Play will begin at Widemarsh at 12 o'clock to-day (Saturday). The elevens will be chosen from the following:—

Mr. R. B. Porch, late of Malvern College,
who plays for Somerset, is tenth in the batting averages
of that club with an average of 16.11. He has scored
203 in 14 innings.

St. John's, in their match on Thursday at Boughton,
against the Club and Ground, took a strong lead after
going in first. They made a capital stand, although
the bowling against them was rather warm. Burrows,
Willoughby, and Ryder shared between them what
wickets fell, before Mr. Young declared with nine
wickets down. Mr. H. V. Plum batted very steadily
for 48. Messrs. Curtis and Mansell also performed
creditably, and 123 was the total. This score looked
like being wiped off, for Burrows was in his smiting
humour and hit up 57 in lively fashion. The County
lot were only 13 behind and six wickets down when
time put a stop to proceedings.

Mr. E. P. Gem bossed the team very well, and I
should think he has acted in a similar capacity before,
although I have not known him do so.

It was rather funny that Straw should have been
objected to by the St. John's captain, because I have
an inkling that he has resorted to similar measures
before, viz., when he has been short of players he has
done the best he could to fill the vacancies. Although
he had a right to object to Straw, who had not fielded,
I think he might have given way, but I suppose it
was his customary zeal in trying to win the match that
made him forget previous circumstances.

The improved state of the ground struck me as soon
as I got there. I subsequently learned that the
brothers J. E. and E. Perkins, both of whom are
independent gentlemen, set to work and levelled 14,000
feet with their own hands last winter. This sub-
stantiates what I have said of them before, that they
are the right men in the right place. This is
enthusiasm indeed, as those who have had a spell at
that sort of work know very well. The wicket was a
perfect one, and, after all the runs which were made,
was just as good at the close.

disputes.context_before:
Rolleston had his annual benefit at Bromsgrove on Saturday, and I hope he will have a substantial sum, for he is a very painstaking cricketer, and immensely popular with the members. He has done well for the club, which is second to none in the district.
I had a good opportunity of looking over the new pavilion, which is one of the best I have seen, and it reflects great credit upon Mr. Gadd, who, I was glad to hear, was getting another ready for the Handsworth Wood Club. Others will sure to follow, for at £115, the total cost, it represents the cheapest and most comfortable one that could be imagined.
disputes.context_after:
I had forgotten to say that there is about £45 yet to be got to clear the pavilion debt, and I notice a match will be played there between 22 ladies and 11 gentlemen. This ought to wipe some of it off, for the tickets are going off well. If the weather is fine there will be a good gate and plenty of fun.
Burrows and Bowley established a record, for they hit up 155 before a wicket fell, and both batted splendidly. The former only just missed his century. Master Caldwell played a perfect innings, and this youngster has only to go on the right way to make a very fine batsman. I like his style very much. The Rev. F. A. Bickmore was batting first rate when the innings was declared. The score had reached 258 for six wickets, and this, against some good bowlers, was capital. I imagine the local team must have felt annoyed that they did not bat first after winning the toss. However, they played a good defensive game, and kept their end up for two hours and a quarter, and made a good draw of it.

I had a good opportunity of looking over the new pavilion, which is one of the best I have seen, and it reflects great credit upon Mr. Gadd, who, I was glad to hear, was getting another ready for the Handsworth Wood Club. Others will sure to follow, for at £115, the total cost, it represents the cheapest and most comfortable one that could be imagined.
The improved state of the ground struck me as soon as I got there. I subsequently learned that the brothers J. E. and E. Perkins, both of whom are independent gentlemen, set to work and levelled 14,000 feet with their own hands last winter. This substantiates what I have said of them before, that they are the right men in the right place. This is enthusiasm indeed, as those who have had a spell at that sort of work know very well. The wicket was a perfect one, and, after all the runs which were made, was just as good at the close.
disputes.context_after:
Burrows and Bowley established a record, for they hit up 155 before a wicket fell, and both batted splendidly. The former only just missed his century. Master Caldwell played a perfect innings, and this youngster has only to go on the right way to make a very fine batsman. I like his style very much. The Rev. F. A. Bickmore was batting first rate when the innings was declared. The score had reached 258 for six wickets, and this, against some good bowlers, was capital. I imagine the local team must have felt annoyed that they did not bat first after winning the toss. However, they played a good defensive game, and kept their end up for two hours and a quarter, and made a good draw of it.
Tommy Straw took off the gloves and went on to, well, I ought to say bowl, but the crowd and the home captain said he threw, and so I suppose he must have done. The circumstance caused a deal of flutter, and John Smith, who was umpiring, had a warm five minutes, but it all finished up in fun. I must warn Tommy to stick to his wicketkeeping, for he has few superiors in that line anywhere.

ROYAL MUNSTER FUSILIERS V ARMY SERVICE CORPS.
BATTING EXTRAORDINARY-THE RECORD BEATEN.
Captain W. Caspe Oates, Royal Munster Fusiliers,
the popular Captain of the Curragh District C.C., and
Private Fitzgerald, of the same battalion, yesterday
had the distinction of topping the batting record by
compiling the immense score of 623 runs during their
partnership, and as both batsmen were not out at the
call of "time," when they seemed good for another 600,
it is impossible to estimate what might have happened
had the game been prolonged. The building up of this
huge score occupied exactly 4½ hours, yielding an ave-
rage of 131 runs per hour. 605 is supposed to have been
the previous record, that being the score credited to
Messrs A. H. Trevor and G. F. Vernon in a match,
Orleans Club v Rickley Green, some years ago, but it is
understood both batsmen were "out." Captain Oates,
who has done so much for cricket, especially for the
ground on which the immense score has been compiled,
richly merits the distinction of having contributed the
lion's share towards this remarkable performance, and
it bears eloquent testimony to the value of the improve-
ments to the ground inaugurated by him eight months
ago, that this new record score should have followed so
closely the score of over 400 runs, recently made by the
Curragh District against Dublin University. Score:-

IRISH CRICKET UNION.
A meeting of the committee of the Leinster branch of
the Irish Union was held last evening in the Wicklow
Hotel, when there were present:-Mr C. W. Frizell (in the
chair), Mr F. Stokes (Dundrum), Mr H. Thornton (Pem-
broke), Mr C. Mitchell (Pembroke), Mr J. Cotter (Dun-
drum), Mr F. H. Browning (Dublin University), hon.
sec. ; Mr J. Foxall (Leinster), hon. treasurer. Mr
Foxall announced that the receipts at the recent Gentle-
men of Ireland v M.C.C. match amounted to £52, and
after the discharge of all liabilities a balance of close on
£30 remained to the credit of the union-a very satis-
factory state of affairs. The Junior Cup competition
was discussed, and it was decided that clubs, in order
to be eligible, should be affiliated with the Leinster
branch by July 1st. Entries for the cup close on July
14th.

disputes.context_after:
Clophill avenged their previous defeat by Ampthill by winning the return game in Ampthill Park on Saturday. J. Taylor figured largely for the visitors, and credit for his side's victory was chiefly due to him for his score of 26 runs and also for taking 7 wickets for 32 runs. For Ampthill, Pickering batted well for 13, but with the exception of the last pair, Sharpe and Penwright, who made 11 each, none of the other batsmen could contribute double figures, and the innings closed for 69. When Clophill batted, J. Taylor scored steadily, and was not dismissed until nearly the end of the game for his 26. Scores:-

People who watched Arnold Sime's fine batting for the Old Bedfordians against Bedford School on Friday and Saturday must have regretted that he is no longer available for the County. When runs have to be got in a hurry Sime is the man for the occasion, and his forcing of the pace in the Old Bedfordians' second innings will long be remembered. The position was this: the Old Bedfordians compiled 314 (Sime 77) in their first knock and got the School out for 187. The School were not dismayed and, following on, scored 203 for nine wickets, leaving the Old Bedfordians with 77 needed for victory. Normally, this would have been an easy task for a side possessing such batting talent as the Old Bedfordians, even in the fourth innings, but time was the important factor. Only thirty-five minutes remained for play.

A Sporting Decision
Doubleday, the School captain, could easily have let his side bat on for a draw, and could hardly have been criticized had he done so, but he unexpectedly declared. This very sporting decision caused quite a stir and put new life into the game. Sime and Oakley hurried out and they proceeded to score regularly off good-length bowling. It was not so much big hitting, but the process of taking cheeky singles and making ones into twos and twos into threes that kept the scorers busy. Both men played nicely-judged strokes and ran intelligently, but it was obvious that Sime was the brains of this partnership.

Captain's Good Service
So much for the people who think that school cricket is dull! Doubleday, the Bedford School captain, may not be a particularly attractive batsman to watch, but he has done yeoman service and has not lacked enterprise in connexion with his leadership. The most successful bowler of the match was (as if he had not already done enough with the bat) Sime. A. E. Cook had the same number of wickets to his credit, but had more runs scored off him. A word or two of commiseration for Harrington, the School wicketkeeper, who had to be replaced because he broke a finger in the early play on Friday. It is wretched luck to miss a game so eagerly awaited.

The Bedford Town first eleven (minus four of their regular players) enhanced their reputation for bright cricket still more when they visited Harrow Town on Saturday. Bedford were late in arriving owing to car trouble which involved nearly half the team, and only four hours' play was possible. However, in these four hours the spectators were treated to some of the most sparkling cricket they have seen this season. Harrow scored freely at the rate of a hundred runs an hour and compiled a very useful 205 for nine wickets.

Harrow scored freely at the rate of a hundred runs an hour and compiled a very useful 205 for nine wickets.
This gave Bedford about two hours of batting in a failing light, but right from the start they went out for runs and were soon on top of the Harrow bowling. E. D. The Bedford Martlets Cricket Club left Bedford this week for their fifth annual tour of Kent. The seventeen members who make up the party have their headquarters at East Farleigh, Maidstone, and the teams to be played are in a thirty-five mile radius of this place. The tour opened with a match against the Royal Marines, Chatham (yesterday), and there is a match on each day (excepting Sunday) until 12th August. The other fixtures will be against Tunbridge Wells, Barming, Whitstable and Tankerton, Frindsbury, Gravesend, Tonbridge, Hythe, and Cranbrook. The touring team is: E. J. Cooper (captain), W. Moore (Cheltenham), E. S. Volz, F. Marshall, D. T. Stevens, H. Steele-Smith (Selwyn College), N. R. Larby (O.B.M.), P. H. Thomas (Selwyn College), K. J. Petts (Welwyn), D. C. H. Wright (Southgate), W. M. E. White (the Army), R. Chatterton (Mill Hill School), V. A. Gubbins (Southgate), N. E. Gillham (Southgate), B. C. Barnwell (O.B.M.), K. C. Campin (Modern School), and D. R. Goodwin (Modern School). In 1938 nine matches were played, of which seven were won by the Martlets.

It will be interesting to see how the young Modern School medium-fast bowler, Campin, fares on the tour. He was outstanding in the School games and captured forty-five wickets—a record number—out of the seventy-six wickets taken. A SPORTING FINISH
Old Bedfordians End their Week

disputes.chosen:
Old Bedfordian Week has come and gone once again, and its enjoyable social events and sporting encounters pass into pleasant memory. The Old Boys beat the boys at cricket—an exciting victory—were beaten by the boys and by the masters at tennis, and had their usual Sunday golf match with the Bedfordshire Club. There were also swimming and rowing contests with the School. On Sunday the annual meeting of the Old Bedfordians Club was held, and the Head Master gave a garden party, and on Friday there was an “At Home” followed by the Old Bedfordians’ Ball, which is reported on another page.
This season’s Bedford School cricket ended on a high note with the two-day twelve-a-side match against the Old Bedfordians. Although forced to follow on, the School struck back to such effect in their second innings that at 6.25 p.m. on Saturday Doubleday, the captain, was in a position to make a sporting declaration. He left the Old Bedfordians with seventy-seven to score in thirty-five minutes. The Old Bedfordians promptly accepted the challenge and sent out Sime and Oakley with instructions to get a move on. And Sime and Oakley did get a move on. They got the runs with some minutes to spare!

The Eleven made an excellent start this season when they put up such a good performance at Luton against Sir Julien Cahn’s strong team. In these days of plumb wickets it is essential, and only fair to the hard-working bowlers, that special attention should be paid, when selecting a team, to the important department of fielding.

August were selected for the County both were still at school, and both made good at once. They are now two of the most consistent players in the side. Another boy, E. D. Markham, who has been showing consistently good form for the newly-formed Bedford Town Club, is having a well deserved trial. If a young player has the ability, plus the right temperament, it is wise to give him a chance with a view to the future.

Two wickets were down for 28 when Barnwell and Bowron began a splendid partnership which added 142 before Barnwell was bowled when only nine short of his century. He gave a fine display of forceful and stylish batting, including fifteen fours. His partner, a newcomer to the Aspley team, was playing in his third match. He was undefeated with 104 when the innings was declared closed at 251 for six. B. C. Barnwell followed up his batting success by a good performance with the ball, taking seven wickets for 44 runs in ten overs. Aspley were easy winners. Scores:-

SPORT OF THE WEEK
Wickets Down Like Nine-Pins — Eagles’ New Players and Plans

disputes.chosen: After ruining outdoor sports engagements on Saturday, it looked as though rain was going to repeat its evil on Monday in the early part of the morning. The main sports fixture was the opening match of the County Cricket Week on the Bedford School playing field against Oxfordshire. The pitch was sodden after the torrential rain of Sunday, but by midday on Monday the weather brightened and a start was made on a newly-prepared crease to the left of the pavilion—away from the School—at about 1.40 p.m. The play that followed was in direct contrast to the weather, being bright and exhilarating to the Bedfordshire supporters. By winning by an innings and 89 runs Bedfordshire made a grand start to the Week. How they fared against Buckinghamshire will be seen by the report in another column.

Wickets Down Like Nine-Pins — Eagles’ New Players and Plans
After ruining outdoor sports engagements on Saturday, it looked as though rain was going to repeat its evil on Monday in the early part of the morning. The main sports fixture was the opening match of the County Cricket Week on the Bedford School playing field against Oxfordshire. The pitch was sodden after the torrential rain of Sunday, but by midday on Monday the weather brightened and a start was made on a newly-prepared crease to the left of the pavilion—away from the School—at about 1.40 p.m. The play that followed was in direct contrast to the weather, being bright and exhilarating to the Bedfordshire supporters. disputes.context_after:
Oxfordshire’s team seemed a strange one to many of us, writes A. R., for so many familiar faces were missing. Territorial camps and other claims had robbed the visitors of old stalwarts and the opportunity was taken of introducing some new blood. The newcomers had an unfortunate introduction to Bedford.
Although it was on the board that the wicket might play tricks later on it was a surprise to see Oxfordshire wickets going down like ninepins in the very early stages. The wicket was as sodden as a pudding and the bowlers had a job to gain a foothold. Yet there were Payne and Oliver having a real bank holiday. Payne bowled Money with the fourth ball of the first over with only one run on the board, and without addition to the score and in the same over the footballer had Parton lbw. Not to be outdone, Oliver sent back Lithgow in his first over, August taking a catch in the slips. Williams, who followed, survived one ball and had his wicket broken with the next from Oliver. Four for two runs, one run being from a no-ball.

disputes.context_after:
“Do-or-Die” Effort
Anyhow Oxfordshire’s sorry plight went on. Two left-arm spin bowlers, Haywood and Owen, the latter bowling over the wicket, replaced the medium-fast attack of Payne and Oliver, and they, too, met with success, but not of such phenomenal order as the opening pair. The ball not turning fast enough to do justice to the wiles of the slow men. With eight wickets down for 28 Oxfordshire wanted a “do-or-die” run, and they had one in O’Shea. While Bowtell went on in a steady, patient way O’Shea tried an aggressive bat. He had all the luck in the world for some time. Owen tied him up in knots without being able to get his wicket. Oliver and Markham had spells with the ball, but it was Haywood who broke the partnership, which put on 56 for the ninth wicket. The Three Counties Hospital player “spun” Bowtell out. The ball almost “stood” before it turned and made the Oxford man give the easiest of catches to Markham. He had scored a valuable 22. O’Shea went on hitting out and compiled 42 not out. It was through him and Bowtell that his side’s total reached 85.

disputes.context_after:
Another Oxfordshire Debacle
Faced with the considerable task of getting 141 runs to avoid an innings defeat, Oxfordshire opened with Lithgow and Peto to the bowling of Payne (School) and Oliver. With the last ball of the first over Oliver induced Lithgow to step across and the batsman was out lbw, one run having been scored. Payne might have had Peto taken in the slips, and then with the score at two Oliver sent a fine ball through Peto’s defence. The total stood at three when the third wicket fell, a ball from Payne taking Parton’s bails. Frequently deliveries from both bowlers reared disconcertingly and Money and Bowtell were anything but easy at the Twice Bowtell almost played on to Payne. At long Oliver had Money caught at stand slip, the Luton bowler having taken three wickets for six runs in three overs and two balls. The first aggressive stroke of the innings was a four to leg by Florey off Payne. Florey decided that an attacking policy was the best in the circumstances and he took thirteen runs off an over by the Chelsea footballer, who was now bowling round the wicket. Florey went on collecting runs by attractive strokes, and he and Bowtell had ridden 27 when the latter was caught at the wicket.

Westrope's eleven batted first, and after losing a wicket at three the captain and K. Marshall took the score to 15. From then on wickets fell fast against some good bowling by R. F. Parker (seven for 12) and H. F. Parker (three for 15), and they were all out for 29.
Pulloxhill suffered an early shock, for W. S. Dollimore was caught at the wicket off the second ball of the innings. E. Ashton and E. H. Parker took the score to 12 before the former was bowled, and then B. Jellis helped the latter to add 4 and was caught. E. H. Parker, after scoring 17, left one run later. A fifth-wicket partnership between R. F. Parker and Ashton saw their opponents' total passed and contributions from the "tail" batsmen helped to make a total of 81.

disputes.context_before:
Bedford Town second team scored another comfortable victory on Saturday, easily defeating the Peterborough second eleven at Newnham Lane. Peterborough batted first and, thanks to some fine bowling by P. Humphreys, they were dismissed for the low total of 74. Humphreys captured seven wickets for 38 runs in eight and a half overs. Last week he took six wickets for seven runs against Royston. The last six Peterborough batsmen added only four runs to the total.
The Town second team began very steadily. Stokes soon mastered the Peterborough bowling, and scoring freely all round the wicket, made a brilliant 66 before being caught in the deep. The Peterborough total was passed with seven wickets in hand, but it was decided to bat on, and when stumps were drawn the Bedford score stood at 121 for seven wickets. The scores were:—

disputes.chosen: St. Neots were away to Stewartby on Saturday, a new fixture, and came away winners by 63 runs, after declaring. St. Neots did not start their innings well, losing the wickets of Owen and Bunnage with only 11 on the board. Craig and Jones batted well, however, and put on 47 for the third wicket before Jones was bowled after making a sound 24, his highest for St. Neots first eleven. After this, four St. Neots wickets fell quickly, but Sillett joined Craig, and this pair added 64 for the eighth wicket. Craig made 67 before being bowled. He batted with great steadiness. Sillett also made his highest score of the season and his 31 included some excellent drives. The St. Neots innings was declared closed at 154 for nine.

Stewartby made an excellent start in their reply, Tysoe and Hudson putting on 55 before being parted, but after the opening partnership was broken the rest of the batsmen collapsed and it was a question as to whether St. Neots would beat the clock and dismiss Stewartby before 7.30, the time fixed for the close of play. With two overs to go St. Neots had still to get rid of two remaining London Brick Company batsmen, but they managed to do it with three balls to spare. Craig, by taking five for 20, completed a good all-round performance for St. Neots. Scores:—

disputes.context_after:
Martlets’ Tour of Kent Nearly Ruined
The Bedford Martlets’ annual cricket tour of Kent was this year nearly ruined by rain. It was not until the last two days that summer weather prevailed. The matches against the Royal Marines at Chatham, K.C.M.H., Barming, and Tonbridge were abandoned without a ball being bowled. The first game at Linden Park, Tunbridge Wells, was played on a wet, but drying wicket, and the Martlets decided to bat after some hesitation. Having practice on concrete at their headquarters the Martlets could not settle down and they were out for 50. Heavy rain threatened to render further play impossible, but a fresh wicket was cut for Linden Park’s innings. Off the first ball N. B. Larby made a catch of Campin (3 for 17) at short leg, and the home side lost three for 10 and four for 28. Rain began to fall again but Linden Park reached 53 for five.

The Martlets, facing their strongest opponents on the County ground at Gravesend, were rather unfortunate to be without W. M. E. White, who was called to Lords to play for the Army against the Public Schools. Before lunch Gravesend took 95 minutes to score 69 runs off some very accurate bowling by Campin and F. Marshall, but in the end they made 246. Campin took five for 60 and K. J. Petts five for 68. Barnwell made a particularly fine catch in the deep. After tea the light became poor and the Martlets lost four for 27. W. Moore (52) and P. R. Thomas (34) made a good stand to save the side. With rain falling the game was given up as a draw, the score being 124 for seven.

The following day was gloriously fine, but at Hythe overnight rain made play impossible before lunch. Hythe sent the Martlets in to bat. Four wickets were down for 17. P. R. Thomas (61) and E. S. Volz (36) put on nearly 100 for the next wicket, and the tail wagged sufficiently to take the score to 152. Hythe were left with 153 runs to make in 105 minutes. Some fine bowling by Campin on a quickly drying wicket banished their hopes. Seven wickets were down for 48, and then a stubborn stand brought the game within ten minutes of the close. A draw looked certain when D. C. H. Wright held a smart left-handed catch in the gully, and the last ball but one from Campin was a beauty and beat the batsman. He took seven for 36. W. M. E. White, who played for Hythe in this game, said that Campin’s bowling was superior to any of the Public School bowling at Lords. Hythe, who lost a batsman through injury, were all out for 78.
The final game, against Mr. Evans’s XI on the Cranbrook School ground, was a curious affair. Before lunch the home team lost eight for 47 against Marshall and Campin, but after the interval the School professional, H. G. Draper, hit a hard 38 and Cranbrook reached 110 (Campin seven for 41, Marshall three for 26). By patient batting W. Moore and Volz took the score to 54, but the absence of Thomas and Barnwell was keenly felt, and the tourists’ total was only 74.

Henlow were beaten by 60 runs at Letchworth on Saturday. Their batsmen, with the exception of R. Lynn and F. Thorogood, failed dismally. Lynn played a grand innings, making 32, including one glorious hit for six. He is regaining his form after his long period of enforced absence. Alexander bowled brilliantly to capture five for eighteen and Grey returned three for thirty. Henlow started off well, Russell bowling Diss first ball, but that was the extent of their success until their total had been passed. Grey and Taylor adding 92 in fifty minutes for the second wicket. Grey, the Bedford Rugby Club full-back, batted brilliantly for his 51, including six fours and a six. Taylor was more subdued in making 28. Fenton, (25) also batted well. A. R. Carlisle, the Henlow skipper, with his tantalizing slows, was their best bowler, taking six for 43. Russell took two for 26. Scores:-

Biggleswade Defeated by Aspley Guise

It was a strange team which took the field to represent Bedford against Hitchin at Bedford on Saturday and the weakened home side gave one of its least attractive displays of the year. Apart from Marston, the Bedford School bowler, and P. Rawlins, the attack was weak; the work in the field was scrappy, and the batting mediocre. Hitchin were unlucky to be denied victory.
Hitchin, batting first, lost a wicket in the second over, but then King and Stanley began an association which put the visitors in a happy position. King hit very freely to score 102, and Stanley was enterprising in making 31, though he made a lot of chancey strokes. Of the batsmen who followed only Brown (35) and Barker (26) were able to face Marston with confidence. This young bowler took six wickets for 46. Rawlins, who got little help from the pitch, did well to take three wickets for 67.

He ran through the London Brick Company, Bletchley, who could total only forty runs on an excellent wicket. In taking eight wickets for eight runs, Barker bowled only six overs, and in his fourth he did the "hat trick". He also captured three wickets in his last over. Webster, at the other end, took the remaining two wickets for 14 runs. Harpur won the match by 91 runs.

There was an exciting finish to the Lynton Works-Kempston game at Kempston on Saturday, the home side winning by one run. Both sides were below strength.
Lynton, batting first, lost three wickets for six runs. Seutchings then joined Everett and helped to put on 14 runs. Curchin (8) and Pestell (7) carried the score along. At this point Everett, who had opened, was out after a very steady innings. The remaining wickets quickly fell and Lynton's final score was 58. For Kempston, Curtis took five for 23 and Cambers three for 10.

A LATE STAND
Saves Flitwick Ramblers

disputes.chosen: When the Ramblers batted J. Godfrey was bowled without a run being scored. Wickets fell very quickly to the fine bowling of A. Palmer and R. Cain, and eight men were out with only 36 runs scored. E. Bonner joined H. Gazeley and they made a stand. While Gazeley did most of the scoring Bonner kept his end up. Gazeley reached his half-century and just later the hundred went up. But with the third ball of the last over H. Gazeley was bowled. The Ramblers' captain's innings included eight fours and one six. His ninth-wicket partnership with E. Bonner realized 76 runs. J. Parker came in to play the last three balls, thus saving the Ramblers from defeat. Scores:-

BEDFORD PICK STRONG TEAM FOR VISIT TO LEICESTER
The “Tigers” Hope that Prominent Men will be Available

disputes.chosen:
To-morrow the Bedford and Leicester
Clubs are due to open the Rugby season
with a game at Welford Road, Leicester,
a fixture that has been played for some
years. At the time of writing the international outlook is still unsettled, and
when these notes are read the shadows
may have darkened or the clouds lifted.
I hope, writes A. R., that the clouds
have gone and that the outlook is
bright. But, international situation or
no international situation, arrangements
are being made to fulfil football programmes and both Leicester and Bedford
have selected teams for their annual clash.
These teams must be governed by the
calls of national defence, but it is hoped that
both clubs will be well represented. Bedford, like their hosts of to-morrow, have
players who are members of the Territorials and defence units, but it is thought
that unless there is a more serious turn
in affairs their men will be able to turn
out. Leicester, on the other hand, have
three first-team men away from the city
on duty now, Barr, Edwards, and Bottrill,
and on Wednesday there was much doubt
whether Herbert and Anthony, two forwards, would be available. However,
optimistic Leicester have included these
players in the fifteen chosen to meet Bedford.

BEDFORD BETTER BALANCED
Let us presume that all is well and look at the sides as though they are sure to turn out as selected. Will Bedford win at Leicester for the fourth year in succession? I think that they will, for their fifteen is better balanced than the “Tigers” team and they will go on the field with the knowledge of three victories to their credit in the last three years. Bedford will be led by Gilbert Cook and he will have a very strong combination to command. The team, which no follower can quarrel about, is as follows: J. E. I. Grey; T. D. Thevenard, J. G. Rogers, E. H. Walshe, and V. J. Lytle; M. E. Staples and R. Smyth; G. T. Danger, B. J. McMaster, G. A. Kelly, R. Wilsher, A. E. Cook, J. G. Cook, H. J. Irens, and O. V. Bevan.

At the time of writing the international outlook is still unsettled, and when these notes are read the shadows may have darkened or the clouds lifted. I hope, writes A. R., that the clouds have gone and that the outlook is bright. But, international situation or no international situation, arrangements are being made to fulfill football programmes and both Leicester and Bedford have selected teams for their annual clash. These teams must be governed by the calls of national defence, but it is hoped that both clubs will be well represented. Bedford, like their hosts of to-morrow, have players who are members of the Territorials and defence units, but it is thought that unless there is a more serious turn in affairs their men will be able to turn out. Leicester, on the other hand, have three first-team men away from the city on duty now. Barr, Edwards, and Bottrill, and on Wednesday there was much doubt whether Herbert and Anthony, two forwards, would be available. However, optimistic Leicester have included these players in the fifteen chosen to meet Bedford.

OPINION UNALTERED
Let us examine the prospects of the Bedford Club in the light of what was revealed at the practice game last Saturday and let me give you one or two news items. First of all the trial impressions. Before the trial it was agreed that the prospects of the Club were bright and, with ordinary luck, another season of high performance was in store. After seeing the trial there is no reason to alter that opinion, which is not one of the usual pre-season optimistic sort based on hope rather than on knowledge. We all knew that the Club, with all last year’s men available, was in a happy position regarding playing strength, and Saturday’s practice revealed that there is an even greater wealth of talent than was expected. Let us take the two key positions at half-back to begin with. How many teams suffer through being poorly served at the link between pack and “threes”? A good many fifteens I’ll wager. Yet look at Bedford. Smyth, Staples, Lovelace, and Kenney (last year’s Leeds University team skipper) are all fitted to take their places at the base of the scrum or at fly-half, where Coleman is also available, not to mention players who normally figure at threequarter who are equally at home there. Likewise at three-quarter and forward the Club has no reason for anxiety with so many promising youngsters ready to challenge for places, and if Grey, at full-back, has the misfortune to get hurt or has to be absent from the team for any other reason, Coleman or Prigmore could well deputize for him. While on the subject of backs, I hear that it is possible Walshe may be joining the Fleet Air Arm, and that being so his appearances with the Bedford side may be limited. He will be missed very much if report is correct. And then there is Jimmy Power, a regular back of last season. I believe it is the Club’s intention to convert him into a forward. He played one game in the pack at the back end of last season and shaped very well. However, his defence as a back was very valuable last winter. Jimmy and his brother George were unable to take part in Saturday’s trial. George is recovering from tonsilitis. Other prominent players who missed the trial included Gilbert Cook, the first fifteen skipper, O. V. Bevan (vice-captain), V. J. Lyttle, D. L. K. Milman, G. T. Danger, A. E. Joy (who will not be able to play at Leicester), D. B. Coleman, C. G. Prigmore, G. L. B. August, and K. V. Percy, and yet the trial was eminently satisfactory. Not because the above players were not there, of course, but because there were so many keen, capable young thoroughbreds on view who kept the better-known players at good stretch. Assistant-Secretary Timmins refereed, and the two sides were in the charge of Rex Wilsher, as fit and wholehearted as ever, and Ralph Spark, the irrepressible, who gets as much fun out of the game as any other two players.

disputes.context_after:
A STRONG ARRAY
Wilsher had a strong array of tried hands under his command including Grey, Thevenard, Walshe, Rogers, Staples, Smyth, Kelly, McMaster, T. Hall, Irens, Black, Western—and there were some lively clashes and strong running. We saw some excellent pieces of work and some first-class tries. Thevenard, by virtue of his speed and indescribable wriggle of the body, having a generous helping of points. Rogers, Walshe, and Staples also crossed the line and both Irens and Grey added goal points with splendidly-judged kicks from wide out. All the old players showed that pace and skill were retained and that little needs remedying with the “bellows”. I don’t propose to go into detail beyond one or two observations on half-back play, which was interesting in view of the competition for places. Smyth, fully recovered from injury, and Staples quickly struck a happy understanding and should be the regular pair for the opening games of the season. Smyth has no equal in the Club for throwing such a long, accurate pass, and he moves quicker (with a long, raking stride) than is imagined. Staples was an outstanding figure at the trial and played with his head as well as his feet and hands. In giving this praise I am not detracting from the performances of Lovelace and Kenney. Lovelace was lively and enterprising, although he did not get so much of the ball as Smyth, and he will need a lot of holding down. He is full of good football. Kenney did not have an extended run at scrum-half, but when in that position he displayed likely form. His passing and generalship were good, but his transfers from the base of the scrum had not the length of the Smyth passes, which can be taken going forward; an important point. So now we must wait for Leicester—some of you Headingley—before we see the team have a real match test. It should be noted that the away fixture with Northampton has been transferred from Saturday 18th November to Thursday 5th October, as the Saturday date clashed with the Leicestershire and East Midlands match with the Australian tourists at Leicester.

disputes.context_before:
Let us examine the prospects of the Bedford Club in the light of what was revealed at the practice game last Saturday and let me give you one or two news items. First of all the trial impressions. Before the trial it was agreed that the prospects of the Club were bright and, with ordinary luck, another season of high performance was in store. After seeing the trial there is no reason to alter that opinion, which is not one of the usual pre-season optimistic sort based on hope rather than on knowledge. We all knew that the Club, with all last year’s men available, was in a happy position regarding playing strength, and Saturday’s practice revealed that there is an even greater wealth of talent than was expected. Let us take the two key positions at half-back to begin with. How many teams suffer through being poorly served at the link between pack and “threes”? A good many fifteens I’ll wager. Yet look at Bedford. Smyth, Staples, Lovelace, and Kenney (last year’s Leeds University team skipper) are all fitted to take their places at the base of the scrum or at fly-half, where Coleman is also available, not to mention players who normally figure at threequarter who are equally at home there. Likewise at three-quarter and forward the Club has no reason for anxiety with so many promising youngsters ready to challenge for places, and if Grey, at full-back, has the misfortune to get hurt or has to be absent from the team for any other reason, Coleman or Prigmore could well deputize for him. While on the subject of backs, I hear that it is possible Walshe may be joining the Fleet Air Arm, and that being so his appearances with the Bedford side may be limited. He will be missed very much if report is correct. And then there is Jimmy Power, a regular back of last season. I believe it is the Club’s intention to convert him into a forward. He played one game in the pack at the back end of last season and shaped very well. However, his defence as a back was very valuable last winter. Jimmy and his brother George were unable to take part in Saturday’s trial. George is recovering from tonsilitis. Other prominent players who missed the trial included Gilbert Cook, the first fifteen skipper, O. V. Bevan (vice-captain), V. J. Lyttle, D. L. K. Milman, G. T. Danger, A. E. Joy (who will not be able to play at Leicester), D. B. Coleman, C. G. Prigmore, G. L. B. August, and K. V. Percy, and yet the trial was eminently satisfactory. Not because the above players were not there, of course, but because there were so many keen, capable young thoroughbreds on view who kept the better-known players at good stretch. Assistant-Secretary Timmins refereed, and the two sides were in the charge of Rex Wilsher, as fit and wholehearted as ever, and Ralph Spark, the irrepressible, who gets as much fun out of the game as any other two players.
A STRONG ARRAY
disputes.context_after:
ACCIDENT TO TREVOR THOMAS
It will be with great regret that Rugby supporters will hear that Trevor Thomas, the Welsh forward who gave such good service to the Bedford Club for several seasons, has had a foot amputated. Trevor, who lives at Woburn Sands, had one foot badly mutilated by machinery at Marston Valley Brickworks at Ridgemont while working on Thursday of last week. He is employed as a panfeeder. The machinery had to be stopped and reversed to release him. He was taken to the Bedford County Hospital, where the foot was amputated.

disputes.chosen: For the first time for some years, Berkshire this season had fixtures with Dorset, who were visitors to the Kensington Road ground at Reading on Wednesday and Thursday. The home county made two changes from the eleven which had played Hertfordshire earlier in the week, M. D. P. Magill, the well-known Army player and R. T. Dedman, a Newbury police sergeant, coming in for A. T. W. Taylor and M. Girling. Once more Stokes was unlucky with the toss, and Berkshire were put in the field. They soon met with success, however, and two wickets were down with only 17 on the board. The rate of scoring was enhanced when Tindall and Carnegie Brown came together, and they carried the score to 75 before the former skied a ball to Wolton at mid-on. One success followed another for Berkshire, for 16 runs later Brown was caught in the slips. Dorset's excellent rate of scoring may be judged from the fact that the hundred was sent up in an hour and a half, and at the lunch interval the score was 121 for five wickets.

BERKS v. DORSET
RAIN AGAIN INTERVENES
disputes.context_after:
Immediately after lunch Dedman brought about something of a collapse among the Dorset batsmen, the remaining wickets falling for the addition of only 21 runs. In fact, the innings was completed in a little over half-an-hour. The seventh and eighth wickets fell without a run being added, as did also the ninth and tenth. Dedman's final analysis ran out at four wickets for 27.
If Dorset had made an inauspicious start and finish, Berkshire were to do even worse. Few of the batsmen appeared to be comfortable, particularly against Bedham, whose deliveries came off the pitch pretty quickly and often popped up. With only one on the board, Berkshire lost their first wicket, and three of them were down for only 16 runs. Not until Crisfield and Cawston got together did runs come with any regularity. The latter got his 25 in eight hits, including a six. Magill rather foolishly threw his wicket away in tempting an almost impossible run. With the score at 74 for 7 at the tea interval, there were hopes of Berkshire at least getting somewhat near the Dorset score, but the remaining Berkshire wickets fell for two runs.

With a wicket down for no score, Berkshire's hopes of getting the Dorset men out cheaply in the second innings were very bright. But things were very soon altered, and by the close of play on Wednesday Dorset had 172 for four wickets.
Heavy rain which fell throughout Wednesday night and for the greater part of Thursday morning caused play to be abandoned, although the players remained at the ground until after the lunch interval in the hope of play being possible. Dorset, therefore, take points for a win on the first innings.

disputes.context_before:
BERKS DRAW WITH HERTS
BERKSHIRE opened their Minor Counties programme on Monday, when Hertfordshire were the visitors to the Kensington Road ground at Reading. It was Hertfordshire's fifth match, however, they having defeated Bucks outright, winning two and losing two of the remaining games on the first innings. Winning the toss, Hertfordshire batted first, but runs came very slowly at the start. It was not until McLean came in that there was any really bright batting. McLean, in fact, took less than a third of the time to compile his 29 than Roberts took for 31. Berkshire bowlers met with little success until Krabbe came on. Although hit about in his first over, he had Roberts caught on the leg side. The score gradually mounted, the best stand being that for the fifth wicket, Kempster and Ford putting on fifty runs. The score would not have been so great had the Berkshire fielders held somewhat easy chances. Ford, who compiled forty, was missed by Bradley off Cawston when only nine, and Wiggs was dropped by Lewis off Relf. It was not until Cawston came on that wickets began to fall with any regularity, and his final analysis was five for 42. Berkshire were greatly assisted by Stokes, who, playing behind the stumps, caught three and stumped one.
disputes.context_after:
An Expensive Miss
This left Hertfordshire with ten minutes to bat before close of play, and Roberts and Tee, although failing to score, played out time. This ten minutes was not without its shocks, however, for Tee was narrowly missed at fine leg. On Tuesday morning Berkshire met with early success, for Relf had Tee l.b.w. in his second over. Roberts and Fordham, however, carried the score to 65 before they were separated. Timewell should have held a lofty catch from Kempster off Girling when the Herts man had only compiled five runs. He went on to score all round the wicket. Girling clean bowled McLean, who had been responsible for some hard hitting in the first innings, and Ford was well run out, Wolton hitting the stumps with a throw-in from the pavilion sight screen. After this Kempster and Ledger remained together to put on 114 runs, Kempster, missed at five, getting a total of 82 before being clean bowled by Cawston. His innings included two sixes—both off Krabbe—and eight fours. Ledger did not stay long after him, succumbing to a brilliant catch by Krabbe, who ran in yards from the boundary to hold the ball almost as it reached the ground. Grimsdell declared the innings closed at three o'clock, leaving Berkshire with three and a quarter hours—should the extra half-hour be demanded—to get 310 runs to win, an almost impossible task.
