SUTTON'S WIN BY FOUR WICKETS
ASPRO'S SPORTING ACTION

disputes.chosen: Played at Cintra on Saturday, and, after an interesting game, ended in a win for Sutton's by 4 wickets, the winning hit being made in the last over of the match. Sutton's won the toss, and decided to put the Aspro in first. This policy was soon justified, as 5 wickets were down for 30, but then Keable and Blackman made a stand, and, with the tail wagging vigorously, they had made 171 when the last wicket fell. Keable played a valuable innings of 61. Anderson bowled 24 overs for 58 runs and 7 wickets—a very creditable performance. Against good bowling by Lund and Butler, Sutton's found runs difficult to obtain, but Cottrell came along with one of his best innings, and with Sayles (33), H. Bradfield (34 not out) and Croom (22) also playing good knocks, they were able to get the necessary runs for victory. This, however, was only possible by the sporting action of the Aspro side, who fielded during the last quarter of an hour in hard rain. Lund bowled excellently to take 4 wickets for 45, while Cottrell's innings of 63 was a splendid effort.

READING SUNDAY v. CHISWICK PRIORY
Played at Earley on Sunday, and won by Reading by 5 wickets. Chiswick Priory won the toss, and, batting first, lost 2 wickets for 16, H. Sharp (51) and F. Ahl (35) then batted well, adding 78 runs before A. V. Percival bowled Sharp. Fifteen runs later the same bowler had Ahl well caught at cover by Bennett, these 2 wickets being obtained at a personal cost of 5 runs in 5 overs. The visitors' total was 159, and Reading did well on a wicket that was taking spin to pass that total with 5 wickets in hand, K. C. Bennett (30) and H. W. Neilan (56 not out) both batting very well.

Apart from Fisher and Pateman, Huntley and Palmers' batsmen put up a very poor show at Newbury on Saturday against the Old Newburians. Huntley and Palmers batted first, and were all out for the poor score of 101 (Fisher 41 not out) and Pateman 32), no one else reaching double figures. Thurkill was the most successful bowler with 4 for 28. The home side found runs hard to get against the bowling of Butler and Carver, and were dismissed for 78, H. and P's winning by 25 runs. Only two of their batsmen managed to reach double figures. Butler took 6 for 57 and Carver 4 for 35.

Berkshire secured two easy wickets, but this brought Catchlife and Peters together to send the score along at a good pace. Peters, who was the top scorer of the match, was missed twice in one over from Bradley before he had reached double figures, first by Relf, who failed to reach a hard chance in the slips, and then by Caudle in the gully. disputes.context_before:
BUCKS BOWLER'S THIRTEEN WICKETS
CONTINUING their Minor Counties cricket programme at the Kensington Road ground, Reading, on Monday and Tuesday, Berkshire put up a sorry show against Buckinghamshire, who were last season's champions. Previous to coming to Reading the Bucks team had done nothing very great this season, having defeated Bedfordshire by two runs on the first innings, and losing by an innings to Hertfordshire. On this occasion Berkshire, failing both from the bowling and batting point of view, lost by an innings and fifteen runs.
disputes.context_after:
Berkshire were left with three and a half hours in which to bat, but in that time they were literally skittled out by Bucks, and also lost four second innings wickets after being forced to follow on. Bucks opened the bowling with Ratcliffe and Lund, the former having four men in the slips, whilst the latter had a leg trap of a similar number. Caudle, this year's Reading School captain, proved to be top scorer of the innings, whilst Owen Sutton came next with nineteen. Sutton, in fact, fully justified his selection by compiling the best aggregate on the Berkshire side. Wolton was the only other Berkshire player to reach double figures. Rutter, the Bucks fast bowler, seemed unplayable to many of the Berkshire men. At one period he had taken four wickets for seven runs, and his final analysis was six for 23. Berkshire were all out for 88, leaving 134 to get to avoid the innings defeat. Although they certainly did better in the second innings they did not succeed in reaching this figure.
Left with 65 minutes for their second innings on Monday Berkshire lost four wickets for 58 runs, and an hour's play on Tuesday sufficed to finish the game. Except for one over by Edwards, Battcock and Rutter bowled throughout this innings unchanged, Rutter securing seven wickets for 55 runs. Some of the Berkshire players showed a tendency to play the ball with their pads instead of with the bat. Bayles was out in the second innings in this way, and Stokes was l.b.w. in both innings. In his second innings Stokes played the first ball he received with his pads, and there was a confident appeal against him. He was given not out on this occasion, but when he did almost exactly the same with the next ball the umpire gave a decision against him. Sutton and Wolton made the best stand, putting on 9 for the fifth wicket. Relf scored about the quickest 21 of the match, and it was a catch by a big hit from him which closed the match.

disputes.chosen: BERKSHIRE staged a splendid recovery in their Minor Counties match against Suffolk at Felixstowe on Wednesday. Batting first on an easy-paced wicket, they made a disastrous start, losing their first three wickets for 27 runs, but the later batsmen attacked the bowling and, thanks to their enterprise, the substantial total of 297 was reached. H. G. Hubble, with 12 fours as his best strokes, batted with admirable skill and initiative for his 88 runs, scored in 100 minutes. Daley, with 7 for 118, was Suffolk's most successful bowler.

disputes.chosen:
Played at Earley on Sunday, and won by The
Ducks by 69 runs. Taking first knock on a wicket
that was very easy before lunch, The Ducks' early
batsmen scored very slowly and carefully, but gave
the side a good start with 106 for 3. Then, 6 wickets
fell for 18 runs, but a last wicket stand added 31,
the total being 155. C. L. Grieshaber (3 for 20) and
A. V. Percival (3 for 32) were the most successful
bowlers. Only three Reading batsmen reached double
figures, Grieshaber (23) being top scorer, and the
whole side was out for 86.

Played at Earley on Monday, and won by Reading
by 39 runs. There had been heavy rain in the
morning, and play did not begin until just before 2
p.m., Reading taking first knock. In two hours the
whole side was out for 82, H. W. Neilan (24), who
was well caught by C. N. West, making the most
runs. A. W. Flatman (6 for 25) had bowled well for
the O.R.s. Then C. J. Woollhead (3 for 16) and
H. W. Neilan (7 for 26), bowling unchanged, dismissed the O.R.s in 84 minutes for 43 runs. To play
out time, each side batted a second time for 45
minutes, Reading again proving the better side with
89 for 5 (Thirkill 38, and Neilan 25 not out), against
42 for 7 (Percival taking 3 wickets for 0 runs in one
over).

disputes.chosen:
Some high scoring was witnessed at Cintra Ground, lent by Messrs. Sutton and Sons, when Berkshire entertained Suffolk for the first time at Reading in the Minor Counties Championship. This was the first county match to take place at Cintra for a number of years. Suffolk fielded a strong eleven, including seven players who had had experience of first-class county cricket, among them being Phil Mead, who played for England and Hampshire.
Winning the toss, Berkshire went in to bat on a very easy wicket. Runs came very rapidly at first, but wickets also fell fairly regularly. Stokes was clean bowled by a short-pitched ball from Belle, whilst Wolton was smartly stumped after going forward to a ball from the same bowler. It was not until Timewell and Crisfield came together that anything of a stand was made. They carried the score to 89 before Timewell put up a high catch in the outfield. Crisfield, who had been missed at four, followed soon afterwards, having contributed a very useful 40 to the score. Hubble started well, but played on to his wicket when he seemed to be getting set. The best batting display was given by Cawston, who in his 98 hit five 6's and eight 4's. He punished Daley very severely, hitting him for three sixes and a four off consecutive balls. Once Cawston had been disposed of, however, the Berkshire tail failed to wag, and the last three wickets fell for the addition of only five runs. Perkins had been the most successful Suffolk bowler.

Berkshire started their second innings disastrously, Stokes being stumped with only two on the board, and Timewell following nine runs later. Crisfield was the next victim, and the Suffolk bowlers seemed to be definitely on top. Until Hubble hit a four off Daley to make the score 26, all of the runs had come in singles. Taylor indulged in some hard hitting, but was given three lives early in his innings, and was eventually bowled by Daley. Relf was caught off the first ball he received. The Berkshire innings closed for 83 runs, and had lasted for only an hour and three-quarters. Perkins had the remarkable bowling figures of six for 15, and altogether had taken 12 wickets for 73 in the match.
With plenty of time in which to compile 102 runs for victory, Suffolk had obtained the runs by the tea interval for the loss of only two wickets. Suffolk, who are at the top of the Minor Counties championship table, have now played six matches, won four, and won one on the first innings, there being no result in one game.

Heavy rain had made the pitch difficult, but by Saturday morning it had dried considerably, and when they went into bat, Berkshire had everything to gain by going for the bowling. Instead, they were content to "nibble" at it, with the result that wickets began to tumble like ninepins.
Sayles had marching orders when the score was only 14, and Stokes left before he had scored. Sayles got out through an in-swinger from Battcock, and Stokes was l.b.w. to the same bowler. Sixteen for three was a poor start, but Hubble rose to the occasion and started to hit out. Partnered by Crisfield, these two sent the score up and up, but after Crisfield had gone, Caudle was out for 9, and the rot had set in. The innings closed at 103.

Two Berkshire County cricketers, O. P. F. Sutton and R. T. Dedman, were awarded their County caps this week for their general performances this season, and particularly for their display against Dorset at Dorchester.
Owen Sutton went to school at Harrow, but, although he played for his house, he did not get his place in the school team. When he left school he forsook cricket for tennis. He was living in Norfolk for a time, and on returning to Reading he took up cricket again, playing for the Reading Cricket Club Sunday eleven and for Sutton's. He had not played for Berkshire prior to this season. He is a keen golfer and is a member of the Reading and Sonning Clubs.

READING v. R.A.F. (UXBRIDGE)
Played at Earley on Sunday, and won by Reading by 5 wickets. R.A.F. (Uxbridge) batted first, and Reading did very well to dismiss a strong batting side for 70 runs in 86 minutes, 7 wickets having fallen before lunch for 58 runs. Machray and Percival accounted for the opening pair in their first over, and J. W. Davis (5 overs, 4 maidens, 4 wickets, 6 runs) and C. J. Woodhead (8.3 overs, 1 maiden, 4 wickets, 22 runs) disposed of the rest of the side. Reading started very badly, losing 5 wickets for 39 in 55 minutes, but G. E. Neilan (43) and H. F. Fox (27) batted very well, and passed the R.A.F. total before being parted. Reading declared at 5.3 p.m. with the score 112 for 9, and R.A.F. (Uxbridge) then showed their batting quality, scoring 144 for 3 in 60 minutes. P/O. J. M. Jewell making 65, including 4 sixes and 5 fours. Reading replied with 100 for 7 in 68 minutes, having again started badly by losing 6 for 36. G. E. Neilan (14 not out) and J. W. Davis (34 not out) got the runs this time, and when stumps were drawn Reading were only 3 runs short of winning the two-innings match.

Try as they would the batsmen could not get the ball away, and with the exception of Hubble, who played a splendid innings under the circumstances, no one stayed very long. Nothing was given away in the field, both the ground fielding and the catching being of the highest order.
Just after 4 o'clock, the whole side were out for what appeared to be a very meagre total.

From the commencement it was seen that even this small total would not be very easy to get. Franklin's wicket fell with only two runs scored. After adding 27 runs Ratcliffe was out lbw and Peters joined Baker, but only six runs had been added when the latter was bowled in trying to hook Dedman.

disputes.context_after:
NORFOLK v BUCKINGHAMSHIRE
BUCKINGHAMSHIRE should have defeated Norfolk at Norwich on Monday and Tuesday, in a match well in keeping with the tradition of these interesting "needle" matches between old rivals. After two or three days' fine weather the pitch was firmer and more suited to good cricket than has been the case lately, and when Bucks won the toss, Franklin had no hesitation in taking first knock. Baker and Franklin opened the innings and runs came steadily against some good bowling by R. C. Rought-Rought and Ballance. With the score at 24, however, Franklin was bowled. Baker showed excellent form, and all bowlers were played with ease and confidence, but just when a long partnership seemed likely, Ratcliffe touched a ball from Langdale and was caught in the slips. When lunch-time came Baker's individual score was 71, and the total 127 for four. Neither Isherwood nor O'Callaghan gave much trouble, and it was left to Baker to push the score along. He completed his century with another boundary. Immediately afterwards he was stumped in trying to drive Ballance. The Bucks innings closed for 194. Probably the quick change from soft wickets to a harder one was responsible for the lack of confidence in most of the batsmen.

D. F. Walker and Theobald opened the Norfolk innings, which was watched with close interest by the Home Secretary, Sir Samuel Hoare, and Lady Hoare. The first over was sensational, as Walker, one of the best amateur batsmen in the country, scored two excellent 4's off Battcock's opening over, and then, misjudging the swing of the last ball, was out lbw. Subsequent play went strongly in favour of Bucks, whose bowlers were on top of their form, often making the ball swing disconcertingly. When eight wickets were down, the score was only 75, but Falcon, the Norfolk captain, and Ballance brought about a complete change. Despite the efforts of all the Bucks bowlers, they kept up their wickets for over an hour, and added 113 runs to the total. It looked as if the Bucks total would be passed when Ballance was caught in the slips off Edwards. The last wicket was obtained without another run being scored, and Bucks thus held a first innings lead of six runs. Bucks went in a second time late in the day and, when stumps were drawn, had scored 22 runs for the loss of Franklin, who was bowled by Boswell.

BUCKINGHAMSHIRE should have defeated Norfolk at Norwich on Monday and Tuesday, in a match well in keeping with the tradition of these interesting "needle" matches between old rivals. After two or three days' fine weather the pitch was firmer and more suited to good cricket than has been the case lately, and when Bucks won the toss, Franklin had no hesitation in taking first knock. Baker and Franklin opened the innings and runs came steadily against some good bowling by R. C. Rought-Rought and Ballance. With the score at 24, however, Franklin was bowled. Baker showed excellent form, and all bowlers were played with ease and confidence, but just when a long partnership seemed likely, Ratcliffe touched a ball from Langdale and was caught in the slips. When lunch-time came Baker's individual score was 71, and the total 127 for four. Neither Isherwood nor O'Callaghan gave much trouble, and it was left to Baker to push the score along. He completed his century with another boundary. Immediately afterwards he was stumped in trying to drive Ballance. The Bucks innings closed for 194. Probably the quick change from soft wickets to a harder one was responsible for the lack of confidence in most of the batsmen.

When the first three wickets had fallen for 36 runs, it seemed as if the whole side would be out for another small total, but D. C. Rought-Rought and Langdale played out time, the score at the close being 86 for 3.
The game was resumed in a damp and misty atmosphere, the outfield being so wet that towels were in demand by the bowlers, who found great difficulty in holding a slippery ball. Norfolk, who wanted 72 runs to avoid an innings defeat, were out for a total of 202, leaving Bucks to score 46 runs for victory. For some unaccountable reason Bucks' early batsmen failed so badly with five of the best out for 30 that it seemed anybody's game. Macindoe and Battcock then confidently met the bowlers until they had carried the score to the necessary total, providing a rousing finish to the match, which completes the Bucks programme for the season. Following the match the teams were entertained at the Countess Wear Hotel when Mr. Dart, secretary to the Gas Co., and Mr. H. G. Read, on behalf of the Brewery, spoke of the way in which such fixtures between sports clubs promoted a better understanding between employees and hoped it would be possible for the fixtures between the Gas Co. and the Brewery to continue. In thanking their hosts for the very elaborate way in which the visitors had been looked after, Mr. Read thought they all ought to be very grateful to Mr. Loynes, hon. secretary of the Gas Co. Sports Club, for the very hard work he must have put in to make the visit such a success.

Winning the toss, Tewkesbury batted first on an easy wicket and Evesham did well to get them out for 115. Their first wicket produced 26 and although two more men left with the addition of only two to the score, runs were afterwards obtained at a steady rate.
H. Robbins and N. Pulley, two medium right arm bowlers, kept a good length and took five for 35 and four for 15 respectively. A new recruit, R. Ingles, of Broadway, a slow left arm bowler, also maintained his length, but bowled with little luck and came out with the analysis of one for 32. Evesham's fielding showed a welcome improvement on last year and Dunn, a new wicket keeper, shaped well.

Bourton Vale suffered their second defeat of the season on Saturday, when they lost to their Winchcombe visitors by two wickets. Batting first, the Vale found run-getting nigh impossible against the fine bowling of T. Headlam, who in 15.3 overs, seven of which were maidens, took seven wickets for 11 runs. **FIVE WICKETS FOR FIVE RUNS!**
Twyning gave an excellent display on Saturday by beating the visiting side, Corse Lawn, by three wickets and 58 runs. Twyning batted first and knocked up 102 for seven, of which S. Healey contributed 51 not out. He was given good support by S. Schofield (13), A. Clements (19), and G. Hone (10). In spite of the considerable total, however, F. Cole (Corse Lawn) managed to take four wickets for only 20 runs, while L. Dudfield, W. Spry and O. Johnson captured one each for 15, 29, and 54 respectively. Corse Lawn had a chance of victory when O. Hartland scored 13, and F. Cole 16. But they failed to keep it up, and gave way under the pressure of S. Healey's excellent bowling. **MATCHES CANCELLED**
The game arranged between Tewkesbury "A" and Evesham "A" was cancelled owing to Tewkesbury ground being unfit due to Friday's heavy rain.
The match between Longdon and Moore Cricket Club was cancelled owing to the latter being unable to raise a team.
**CAPTAIN'S TEAM BEATEN**
Bushley commenced its season on Saturday with a match between the captain's (E. E. Bisley) eleven and the sub-captain's (C. Walker) team, and after a pleasant and exciting game resulted in the latter team (although a man short) winning by one wicket and five runs. The captain's team went in first, and half the side was out for 33. S. Hunt was in good form, however, and contributed 22 (including a 6 and two 4's). The last man (J. W. Day) scored a valuable 14, and the team was dismissed for 85. C. Fowler was in good form with the ball, and captured the first four wickets for 15 runs; F. Mayo had three for 12; and P. Townsend three for eight. P. Hart and W. Barnes opened the account for the sub-captain's team, and thanks to the latter, 32 was on the board before a separation was effected. Thirty additional runs were on the score before the next wicket fell, and the fielding side looked like being beaten very badly. However, a slump took place and the following six wickets added 26 only. But this was sufficient to gain victory, Barnes contributed 40 not out, including five 4's; and J. F. Fowler scored 17. E. E. Bisley, for the captain's eleven, captured four wickets for 23, and J. W. Day, three for seven.
**OVERBURY BEATEN AT HOME**
Overbury and Buckland and Laverton opened their season on Saturday when they met at Overbury, the visitors winning by 12 runs. Batting first, Buckland knocked up 73, G. Hacklett hitting a useful 38. Bryant (4 for 21), H. Green (4 for 26), and J. Collis (2 for 12).

Ripple entertained Worcester Nomads on Saturday, and in a low-scoring match, won by nine runs. It was definitely a bowler's match, as is revealed by the analyses.

disputes.chosen:
**HASFIELD AND TIRLEY LOSE FIRST GAME**
Hasfield and Tirley opened their season on Saturday by being defeated at Norton by one wicket and 19 runs.
The visitors, who took first knock, began moderately well, T. Dudfield and D. Barnes scoring 19 between them. The scoring rather sagged after this, and five wickets were down for only 27 runs. L. Bond contributed another ten, and the remaining batsmen being out, the visitors closed their innings with a total of 44 only.
Norton's victory was in no small measure due to the 23 runs contributed by A. Bradshaw, because no other player with the exception of A. Maycott (12 not out) reached double figures. The issue was put beyond all doubt with three wickets in hand, and the Norton score closed at 63 for nine.
For Norton, F. Wheeler had the splendid analysis of six wickets for 10, L. Gardiner capturing the remaining four for 14 runs.
No fewer than seven bowlers were tried by the visitors, of whom G. Didcote was most successful with four wickets for nine; J. W. Bartlett had three for 12, and W. Steward and T. Dudfield one each for eight and nine respectively.
**FORTHAMPTON C.C.**
As it was found impossible, owing to lack of players, to carry on Forthampton Cricket Club this season, the fixtures have been cancelled. At a meeting of members on Wednesday evening, an inventory of the spoilt view to their being disposed of, but it was stated the club was only in abeyance, and it was hoped that it would be re-started in the future. Meanwhile, it was decided that the assets of the club should be invested in the hands of one or more trustees, so that, if revived, it would have a sound financial basis.

FORTHAMPTON C.C.
As it was found impossible, owing to lack of players, to carry on Forthampton Cricket Club this season, the fixtures have been cancelled. At a meeting of members on Wednesday evening, an inventory of the spoilable cricketing materials was made, with a view to their being disposed of, but it was stated the club was only in abeyance, and it was hoped that it would be re-started in the future. Meanwhile, it was decided that the assets of the club should be invested in the hands of one or more trustees, so that, if revived, it would have a sound financial basis.

Mr Kitcat had another memorable experience with Dr. W. G. Grace. He was in the team during that wonderful May, 1895, when the "Old Man" made cricket history by scoring 1,000 runs before the month was over. Frys batted first, and thanks to A. Woolacott (64, not out), and L. H. Carter (36), they totalled 130. Then the Bohemians made a poor start, losing two wickets for a few runs, but A. Bull (21), C. R. Lucas (38), and H. J. Alpass (34), pulled things round. However, the bowlers got on top again, and with the last pair together it was anybody's game. Amid great excitement R. F. P. Holloway levelled the scores, but in attempting the winning run, the last man was run out, and the game ended at 130 runs apiece. P. W. Setchell, and R. D. French took four wickets for 28 runs, and three for 21 respectively, for Bohemians.

Marriott, who took 6 wickets for 22 runs in eight overs, bowling well, St. Albans dismissed the Old Boys for 85, a collapse ensuing after the sixth wicket fell at 74. L. O. KING'S "HAT TRICK."
L. O. King, of Radlett, performed the "hat trick" for the Herts County Club on Friday, when they beat St. Albans by 184 runs. Taking seven wickets for 33, he was mainly responsible for St. Albans' cheap dismissal. King also batted well, his 67 being the top score of the game. The Country Club lost two wickets for 14, but J. A. R. Oliver (56) and King, whose partnership realised 104, won the game without further loss.

Northmet (St. Albans) beat Frogmore by eleven runs at Park Street, on Sunday. They made 86, of which R. Levin (26 not out) and J. Smith (4) contributed 50 in a last-wicket stand. O. Butler (21), B. Smith (15), D. P. Hollingsworth (10) made most of the runs previously. Wright (4-18) and J. England (4-34) did best with the ball for Frogmore, while L. Lee (25) batted well, but the rest of the side did badly until W. Lee (18) and A. Rimmonds (5 not out) put on 27 for the last wicket, which lifted the total to 75. F. Runchiman (5-17), L. Morley (3-18) and D. Hollingsworth (3-19) bowled steadily for Northmet.

Radlett beat Hampstead by 33 runs at Cobden Hill, on Saturday. ENTERPRISING ELSTREE.
Elstree's fixture with Edgware, on Saturday, was scratched, but Elstree were able to fix up another game with West Herts II., whom they defeated by five wickets. West Herts took first knock, but their early batsmen scored slowly and eventually a declaration was made with 129 for 9. Elstree went for the runs, and passed West Herts' total for the loss of five wickets. W. H. Ribout (49), A. Lyons (44) and D. H. Attewell (36) batting in enterprising fashion. E. Evans, who took 5 wickets for 16 in fifteen overs of which eight were maiden, again bowled well for Elstree. Scores:-

BATSMEN took a back seat and bowlers blossomed into brilliance in club cricket during the week-end. In contrast to recent weeks not a single century was scored, although F. Richards, of Stanmore, came preciously near to that distinction with a well hit 95. These runs were gathered at the expense of the Ickenham attack. Another Stanmore player, K. H. Chapman, against Radlett, put up about the deadliest turn of wicket destroying bowling seen on the Common for some time. Taking a wicket with the first ball of the match, he bowled for five overs without conceding a run, and secured five victims. His final analysis was:

WELWYN GARDEN CITY 32 .. ABBOTS LANGLEY 90
ABBOTS LANGLEY'S victory at Welwyn by 58 runs on Sunday was chiefly due to the remarkable bowling of A. W. Briers, who, in the course of seven overs, captured six wickets for nine runs. He was ably supported by R. Crownshaw, who in eight overs secured four wickets for 21 runs.

disputes.chosen:
ABBOTS LANGLEY'S victory at Welwyn by 58 runs on Sunday was chiefly due to the remarkable bowling of A. W. Briers, who, in the course of seven overs, captured six wickets for nine runs. He was ably supported by R. Crownshaw, who in eight overs secured four wickets for 21 runs.
Abbots Langley batted first, and were soon in difficulties with O'Brien, who bowled magnificently in capturing six wickets for 19 runs. A. W. Briers and C. Sharp saved the situation with scores of 25 and 27 respectively, but even so, a total of 90 appeared insufficient. However, the home batsmen were unable to cope with the Briers—Crownshaw combination, and were dismissed in 54 minutes for a meagre 32. Score:—

disputes.context_before:
WEST HERTS AND WATFORD OBSERVER: FRIDAY 11 AUGUST 1939-2.
HEMPSTEAD GET OPPONENTS OUT TWICE
disputes.context_after:
Although rain delayed the start until nearly 3.30 p.m., Hemel Hempstead found plenty of time in which to comfortably defeat Wimbledon Crusaders on the Heath Park ground on Monday. The visitors, batting first, could only muster 45, Brandon taking six for 15 and Capel four for 26.
Hemel Hempstead started strongly, and 81 runs were on the board before the first wicket fell. The total was taken to 150 for the loss of only two more wickets, Grange contributing a sound 54 before being run out and Wallers hitting 56, including six fours and two sixes, before being caught on the boundary.

disputes.chosen: No cricket was possible at Rickmansworth over the Bank Holiday until 4 o'clock on Monday. The match had been scratched at lunch time, but the weather improved, and the captains decided to make a start. The Rickmansworth team was made up at the last minute (as several people had left the ground at lunch time), and they could only find nine batsmen. Old Spicers batted first and made 91, the last wicket putting on 27. Murray hit 2 for 37 and Edmunds bowled well, taking seven for 21. When Rickmansworth batted Marriott played well for 29, and with Chicken had the best stand of the day, but Rickmansworth were all out for 74, losing by 17 runs. Score:

YATES GETS 1,000 RUNS WITH "OBSERVER" BAT
On Sunday Don Yates, the Odhams and North Watford Conservatives prolific batsman, reached his thousand runs for the season. He has accomplished this feat in 23 innings, and has used an "Observer" prize-winning bat, which he won last year. "I have never had a better bat," he said yesterday. "The one I won last year drives beautifully, and I am certainly anxious to get another."

Olsson (57) gave the Old Berkhamstedians a good start, but after they had been separated wickets fell quickly, the ninth falling when the Old Boys were 42 in arrears. Fltoot and Houghton, however, defended doggedly to save the game. Scores:—

ST. ALBANS' FINE VICTORY AT LUTON.
disputes.context_after:
St. Albans batted first, but A. S. Hacker (219) and S. H. Rabone (43) were the only players to reach double figures against good bowling, particularly by R. B. Webb (7 27). St. Albans had eight men out for 64, but C. J. Holt (3 not out) played very steadily to keep his end up while S. H. Rabone added 23 for the ninth wicket.
Luton lost both their opening batsmen at nine. With F. Minshull (3 - 21), J. Holt (2—27) and S. H. Rabone (1—10) all bowling effectively five wickets were down for 36 and seven men were out for 51. A. J. Burboys aided by C. J. Partridge tried hard to pull the game round. When they had raised the score to 70, Burboys, who had made 36, was caught by Weatherhead off Lismore (3—10), who finished off the innings for the addition of three runs by taking a return from Webb and getting Emery lbw. OLD ALBANIANS' SURPRISING COLLAPSE.
The Old Albanians suffered a sensational one-run defeat on Saturday, when they opposed Shenley Hospital at Porter's Park. Shenley, thanks largely to a good knock of 42 by A. Clarke, totalled 98. M. A. Wiggs (56), A. G. Owen (18) and K. A. Griffiths (16) gave the Old Boys a capital start; indeed they needed only nineteen for victory when the fourth wicket fell, but Brown (4—38) and Woodcock (2—21) brought about a surprising collapse. Eight wickets were down for 99. The ninth lifted the total to 97 and two runs were still required when W. Fenton, the last man, went in, but he was caught by Greenhaugh of Brown without addition to the total and Shenley succeeded, in a tense finish, by one run. Scores:—

HARPENDEN WEDNESDAY'S ESCAPE.
Harpenden Wednesday's home game with Tring Park was left drawn. Harpenden, who made 130, could do little with the bowling of A. Kempster (6—46). Tring Park lost five wickets for 62, but then L. Sandridge again disappointed their supporters on Sunday by losing their home game with Hadlett Wednesday by 44 runs.
Dismissed in ten overs for 32, no member of the Sandridge team reached double figures, Cautsin (9) and Roan (8) being top scorers. Hadlett scored 26 of the necessary runs before the first wicket fell, Sampson going on first change then secured 3 wickets for 6 runs, finishing up with 4 for 12. W. Lamb subsequently hit out, and he and Hemslcy added 21 for the last wicket. The fact that two Sandridge players one their principal run-getter and the other who was holding up his end nicely were run out had disastrous effect on the side, but the bowling of Brennan was exceptionally good, as his figures, 5—13, show. Scores:-

A SETBACK FOR ELSTREE.
Elstree lost unexpectedly to the Old Johnians on Saturday. E. Evans (6—32) was in great form with the ball and the Old Boys, who batted first, had a disastrous time. The first wicket fell at 11 and seven men were out for 14. P. Lumley (10) helped E. Keeton (36) to stop the rot, but the eighth wicket fell at 24. J. Stieb (15) and Keeton put on the total of 48 for 9, and J. Leach, who made one not out, kept his end up while Keeton lifted the total to 74 before being bowled by J. Milner.

Thanks to a fine innings by A. Vass (46), Westbourne passed the Markyate total with eight wickets in hand, but bowlers got on top after that. A. Batting first the Referees were dismissed for 35, A. C. Sampson obtaining 4 for 8, Winch 2 for 6, Atkins 1 for 0 and Caustin 1 for 9. DON YATES, who is the terror of every local bowler, hit his 44th century on Saturday. Since 1928, when he started his brilliant career with Watford Clarence, Yates has been a prolific scorer. With Oxhey Grange, Waterlows, Odhams and North Watford Conservatives, he has hit 1,000 runs (or more) each year since 1929. He has already reached this number this season. One summer on behalf of Waterlows his tally reached 2,000.
His average to date for this wet summer is 67.
What a great pity it was that Yates's talents were not recognised, and some effort made to give him an opportunity to develop in a higher class of cricket. It is obvious that Yates has exceptional ability, and would have made his mark in higher company had he been brought along on the right lines.
It seems a crying shame that such talent is wasted—it wouldn't happen in Australia.
The excellent batting of W. Townley, of Kings Langley, has been attracting a lot of attention. He is well worth a trial for the county. Less able players often appeared. An indication of this young man's ability was furnished on Saturday when he carried his bat for 19 against Berkhamsted — not great score, it is true, but his innings won the match for his side. A type of opening bat that is rare in club cricket. Townley is dependable, thorough and workmanlike.

KINGS LANGLEY'S journey to Digswell Park on Saturday resulted in a drawn game. Batting first Welwyn put together a score of 177 for seven wickets, an excellent second wicket partnership between Carter and Pakes putting on 97 runs. With the first ball of his second spell Mills bowled Carter, and in the course of a further five overs dismissed six of the Welwyn side for 26 runs, giving him a final analysis of six for 57.

IN the ideal cricket weather that only the start of the football season can bring, few matches were brought to a definite result. Abbots Langley preserved their unbeaten record by the skin of their teeth, beating Chipperfield by eight runs, Hemel Hempstead won very comfortably, but West Herts, Bushey, Chorleywood, Stanmore, Leavesden and Kings Langley were among the teams that drew their fixtures.
Of the five centuries that were scored, Don Yates obtained two—hitting 108 not out on Saturday, and 100 not out on Sunday. Yet another Yates achievement.
The best individual performances were as follows:
BATTING
G. FLOYD (West Watford Conservatives) v. Northwood British Legion 119.
D. YATES (Odhams) v. Rembrandt—108*.
M. B. FAITTFLLI (Bushey II) v. Chorleywood II—105.
G. BLOICE (Sun Engraving) v. Amersham Paper Mills—101.
D. YATES (North Watford Conservatives) v. Ogee Sports—100*.
* Denotes not out.
BOWLING
R. BRANDON (Hemel Hempstead) v. Leighton Buzzard—7 for 28.
H. FORD (St. John's) v. Leavesden-road Baptists—6 for 5.
F. ENGLAND (Bricket Wood and Munden) v. Garston—5 for 5.

disputes.context_before:
A. KING’S 102 IN 88 MINUTES
Time Thwarts Hitchin at Bedford
disputes.context_after:
Opposing Bedford, on the latter’s ground, Hitchin had an early shock when J. D. Waters was ibw to Kenney for a duck with only one run on the score-board. W. V. Stanley then helped King to take the score to 132 before being caught, and when King left four runs later he had made 102 out of the 138. Subsequently Sid Brown made 35 (which included six boundaries) and Barker hit five four’s in a useful contribution of 26, so that Hitchin finally totalled 222.
D. D. Audley, who opened for Bedford with R. Kenney, played a grand fighting innings of 52 before being run out with the score at 109 for four wickets, but five more wickets fell while 15 runs were being added, and Hitchin looked like snatching a thrilling victory. However, they were thwarted by a last-wicket stand by R. Hawkes and R. Ferriman, and had to be content with a draw, though they held the overwhelming lead of 83 runs when stumps were drawn.

KIMPTON’S POOR SEASON.
In their last home game, Kimpton suffered a heavy defeat against Luton Boys’ Club, and from a results point of view they have had an unusually poor season. Bowling unchanged for the visitors, Matthews and Jones ran through the Kimpton team for the meagre score of 45, and only Gerald Cain, who hit a six, got double figures. Slack fielding was partly responsible for the Luton team making 80 for five wickets, although two of their players were run out in attempting to steal short runs.

team. Like our other bat-men, he had long spells of low scoring, but his three centuries were an exhibition of sparkling cricket. When out to make runs, Chalk, Valentine and Ames are a treat to watch. No other county possesses such a trio.
When young Peter Foster came into the team a good many judges of the game said he was not quite up to first-class form and in the first three matches he lived up to this reputation. In the middle of the season, however, he greatly improved and his 107 against Leicester was a delightful innings. You could not at present call his defence very sound, but he possesses some charming strokes.
Todd has maintained his position as the most valuable all-round man in the eleven. If anything he has been over-bowled and it must be remembered that he is the first to attack against the host batsmen. His batting has naturally suffered, but at times he has heroically stopped a collapse and three centuries. A fine record.
The rest of our batsmen have been disappointing. Wright and Harding have not come up to expectations in that part of the game.
Coming to the bowling, we find Wright far ahead of the others. At times he simply slaughtered batsmen. He has increased his pace this year and the quickness with which his break comes in from the leg has upset the best batsmen.
Watt has done well at times with his shorter run and slower deliveries. Harding has improved upon last year and next year, if there is cricket, he will be more deadly. Lewis greatly improved and when Wright was away in the Tests did wonderfully well. It is worth his while to practise batting. The other bowler to mention is J. W. Martin, the Catford amateur fast bowler. Given more practice in county cricket he should improve.
Thus we come to an end of the cricket season of 1939—a tragic end. Let us hope and pray that county cricket will be played again next season.

Generally speaking I can only repeat what I have continually said during the season-that as a whole our bowlers have been more consistent than our batsmen. No really big scores have been amassed against us. In Levett we have had a first-class wicket-keeper and have suffered in no way from the absence of Ames behind the stumps.
In regard to the leading batsmen, we have never known what each would do. One of them might play in a couple of matches and never get into double figures, then he would burst forth with a century, or even two. Absolute inconsistency. But it shows the fascinating uncertainty of cricket.

Ames started in a similar way to Fagg. In his first thirteen innings this season he totalled only 245 runs. Then against Glamorgan he made 177. He had other spells of low scoring, followed by a century, but looking at his batting for the whole season, he must be placed as the most reliable of our eleven. No-one who saw it will ever forget his wonderful performance at the Oval when he made 136 in 68 minutes and won the £100 annually given to the batsman who makes a century in the quickest time.
Next in the averages is R. H. Valentine, and here again we had splashes of brilliance interspersed with failures. He is one of those batsmen feared by the opposite side. When once he gets going all bowlers seem powerless, but his great failure is a desire to start scoring a little too quickly, and for that reason he has lost his wicket many a time in the first few overs.

The Kent skipper, F. G. H. Chalk, has the courage to take an independent course quite contrary to the policy of most captains. He has been criticised for putting in Yorkshire at Dover and also neglecting to make Sussex follow-on at Hastings. In one case he was successful, but in the other, at Dover, it was a definite failure.
Chalk is a great personality in the field, always alert and beloved by the whole team. Like our other bat-men, he had long spells of low scoring, but his three centuries were an exhibition of sparkling cricket. When out to make runs, Chalk, Valentine and Ames are a treat to watch. No other county possesses such a trio.

Chalk is a great personality in the field, always alert and beloved by the whole team. Like our other bat-men, he had long spells of low scoring, but his three centuries were an exhibition of sparkling cricket. When out to make runs, Chalk, Valentine and Ames are a treat to watch. No other county possesses such a trio.
When young Peter Foster came into the team a good many judges of the game said he was not quite up to first-class form and in the first three matches he lived up to this reputation. In the middle of the season, however, he greatly improved and his 107 against Leicester was a delightful innings. You could not at present call his defence very sound, but he possesses some charming strokes.
Todd has maintained his position as the most valuable all-round man in the eleven. If anything he has been over-bowled and it must be remembered that he is the first to attack against the best batsmen. His batting has naturally suffered, but at times he has heroically stopped a collapse. And three centuries. A fine record.
The rest of our batsmen have been disappointing. Wright and Harding have not come up to expectations in that part of the game.
Coming to the bowling, we find Wright far ahead of the others. At times he simply slaughtered batsmen. He has increased his pace this year and the quickness with which his break comes in from the leg has upset the best batsmen.
Watt has done well at times with his shorter run and slower deliveries. Harding has improved upon last year and next year, if there is cricket, he will be more deadly. Lewis greatly improved and when Wright was away in the Tests did wonderfully well. It is worth his while to practise batting. The other bowler to mention is J. W. Martin, the Catford amateur fast bowler. Given more practice in county cricket he should improve.
Thus we come to an end of the cricket season of 1939-a tragic end. Let us hope and pray that county cricket will be played again next season.
